subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN TITLE FROM "DOMINION" TO "STATE"
speechtext:
Just a brief explanation, Mr. Speaker. Several hon. members are wondering where the expression dominion comes from. In itself, that expression carries no aggressive connotation. But in the province of Quebec we always hear references to the state of Quebec, and the provincial ministers have decided that in future, the only name they would use to call the Quebec government would be the state of Quebec.
Now, in view of section 3 of the constitution, Canada is a dominion.
What I cannot conceive or explain, Mr. Speaker, is that since Quebec is supposed to remain part and parcel of Canada, how could the part assert itself with more independence than the whole?
The dominion carries a bond of subordination. We are proud of our great country, Canada, and since we want our country to assert its sovereignty on a factual as well as on a symbolic basis, I thought that from now on we could say that Canada constitutes a federal state.

The hon. member is an avowed republican and is aiming at establishing a republic in this country. I think unless we are absolutely clear about that which is in this proposed bill we should not accept it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the secretary general of the United Nations is back in New York, but I was not able to get in touch with him this morning. All I can go by is the reported statement which he made as to his interview with Chairman Khrushchev.
I suspect that what is reported is correct. However, it does not necessarily follow that the situation will result in circumstances that would warrant the course indicated by the head of the government of the Soviet union. It is true that under article 19 of the charter, if a country is delinquent in an amount greater than its total assessment of the previous two years, that country, as the result of a vote in the general assembly, does qualify for the withdrawal of its voting privileges. However, article 18 of the charter has yet to be applied. It may be that this under the procedures of the UN which will be regarded as an important question might prevent any encouragement of the action that the Soviet union has announced it would take.
As far as the government of Canada is concerned, it believes strongly that all countries great and small, which are in a deficit position, should pay off their obligations to the UN. In the case of the Soviet union this obligation runs close to $60 million. That indebtedness, together with other obligations, represents a very severe burden on the United Nations. The attitude of the Canadian government on this question is that we hope no confrontation will occur and that the Soviet union will recognize that, if it is sincere in its support of the United Nations, it should take action that will not make it necessary for nations to give consideration to the implications of article 19.

I am pleased to have an
opportunity to speak today. There were so many others who wished to speak on Friday that I was unable to maintain my place.
Today I intend to make a few remarks in respect of citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs. As hon. members are aware, I am very interested in citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs because my constituency of Vegreville includes the Saddle lake Indian reserve. Individuals from approximately 40 nations of the world live in my constituency, and all from time to time have difficulty with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
I feel it very necessary that the citizenship and immigration acts be amended to make it possible for individuals sponsored by relations other than brothers and sons to enter Canada. Even a sister sponsored by a brother cannot enter this country. It strikes me as very strange indeed that so much difficulty is encountered by individuals desiring to come to Canada at this time when Canada so very badly needs an increased population. Can you feature a country of this size having a population of approximately 19,330,000? Canada should have a population of at least four times that figure, and I am sure can support such a population. I am sure no one would question that suggestion. I am sure with a population of that size Canada's production would be used and there would be less unemployment, because the
Interim Supply
requirement then would be such that these people would all be employed to meet the increased demand.
While the United States is not plagued by unpleasant weather and conditions of that nature that beset parts of our country, it has a papulation ten times the size of our population. I am sure Canada could support a population four times its present size. I am also sure the population cannot be so increased without bringing people from other countries of the world. People from every nation in the world desire to come to Canada. While some of them may not be welcome, I suggest we would be happy to accept the vast majority. I am sure we could provide homes and a living for them without having to beg support from the government.
On many occasions, both in this house and in letters to four or five ministers of citizenship and immigration over the past several years, I have made representations with respect to changing the practices followed by the citizenship and immigration department. Nothing has been done as yet, though I hope I will soon be able to contact a minister in favour of granting citizenship to the type of individual to whom I have referred in previous speeches. There is a young lady who has lived in this country since 1939 and who has taught high school for 12 years. This young woman cannot obtain citizenship in spite of the fact that the judge of the citizenship court in the city of Edmonton has recommended on five separate occasions that she be granted citizenship without question. I cannot be told why she has been unable to obtain citizenship. I am only a member of parliament, just a backbencher in the highest court in Canada. In the name of heaven why cannot we and these people be told the reason they cannot get citizenship?
This is only one case. There are people in Poland and other countries who want to come to Canada. They cannot do so because the person who wants to sponsor them is an uncle. Can you imagine anything so stupid as that? They are not closely enough related. Is that not a silly thing? One wonders how we can be so stupid in framing our immigration laws. At one time it may have been thought that we were protecting Canada by being so stuffy about our immigration laws. I do not believe we should be so terribly careful any more.
In this country we have a great many people who do not look upon government as we do. There are many who are communists. Seven years ago, in the election of 1957,
