there were 973 people in my constituency who voted communist. In the last election there were only 455. Do you think those people are doing my constituency any harm? Certainly they engage in some propaganda, but I do not think we should be so tough on them when they have lived in Canada practically all their lives. They are Canadians too. They simply have a slightly different outlook. They go a little farther in their views than my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is an avowed socialist, or the squire of the Kootenays, the hon. member for Kootenay West, who is also an avowed socialist. If the chips were down neither of them would be any more socialist than I am.
I think people should be allowed to own what they work for. Free enterprise is what has made Canada, and if somebody looks at thinks a little differently from the two original political parties in this country they may have something. They cannot be altogether wrong. So I think we should be a little less stuffy about our method of granting citizenship to certain Canadians who have proved that they are Canadians.
There should be an effective citizenship appeal board in this country. I know there is one that is called on at times to help the minister, but there should be a citizenship appeal board which could listen to the appeals of people like the young lady to whom I have referred, who has been turned down five times. Her latest application is before the minister. I have tried to find out what has happened, but he has told me very nicely he will let me know when a decision has been made. There should be an appeal board to which this girl and the many others in similar circumstances could apply rather than having to apply to the minister. There should also be a body other than the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which would make the final investigation of a person applying to the appeal board for citizenship. The R.C.M.P. does a wonderful job in its initial investigation of applicants for citizenship, but when appeals are necessary there should be another body to do this work.
I will leave that issue there and turn to the department of Indian affairs. To my mind there should be a separate minister in charge of Indian affairs, not the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. If he does his job as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration properly, believe me he has plenty to do without looking after the big job of Indian affairs. The superintendent general of Indian

affairs should be a person who has Indian affairs as his main job, and it should not be a secondary job which is approached with the attitude that if matters are looked after today, well and good; but if not tomorrow will do.
I want to make a few remarks about the Indian claims commission. We have heard a great deal about this commission. The former minister in charge of Indian affairs, now Minister of Justice and house leader, suggested that legislation to establish an Indian claims commission would be brought before the house long ago. So far very little has been done about the matter. I believe it was announced at one time that there was a cut-off date for the registering of Indian claims. If the Indian claims commission does not get going soon, how in the name of heaven are we ever going to resolve the troubles of the Indians if there is nobody to listen to their claims? Every Indian band in the country has a claim to make against the government of Canada or a provincial government. The claims commission should be established and put into operation right away.
On the claims commission we must have Canadians who know the Indian problem and who can look at things the way an Indian does. You require people who have lived among the Indians and know what they are talking about. The Indians themselves claim there should be a qualified anthropologist on the commission to look into their origin. Because they ask for this I suppose we should have it, but personally I cannot see exactly why we need to have such a person. Many of the tribes I have talked to have referred to a certain individual from another country, but I will not mention any names today. I cannot see why the Indians, of all people, should want somebody who is not a Canadian citizen to pass on their claims for redress of offences allegedly committed by the government of Canada or the provincial governments.
At the time the former government was defeated the Indian Act was in the process of being remodelled. It is high time that the remodelling was put into effect. The idea the former government had of submitting changes to the Indians for their approval was a very good idea. The Indians must be consulted about any changes to be made in legislation which concerns them. They are the original settlers of this country, and they should not be pushed aside and forgotten.

There are many things connected with the administration of reserves that must be changed. I feel that the Indian superintendents, the people whom we used to call Indian agents, should be North American Indians who are trained to be Indian agents and to look after these reserves. This is something that is necessary. In so far as the Saddle lake reserve in my own area is concerned-there are six or seven reserves under the one agent-I must say that we have at St. Paul, Alberta a superintendent who is or was a treaty Indian. He has done a marvellous job since he came there about two years ago. I have not heard within the last month or two whether he is still there, but I hope he is. Somehow I am not told as often as I used to be what is happening on the reserve, nor as soon as I used to be. In any event, I feel that people who administer Indian reserves should be Indians, because they are familiar with the outlook of their people and are able to deal with it.
Indian reserves should have access to electricity. They can get electricity now through the use of their revolving fund if they pay 25 per cent of the loan as a deposit. I feel that when they have this revolving fund they ought to be able to get the full amount of the loan from the revolving fund, and then they can start to repay it. So far as my reserve is concerned, these are very good people. They are honest and they are industrious, in the main. Some of them are not too industrious but the vast majority are. They would pay off a debt like that without too much difficulty, because they are willing to work at all times and they get good pay. Some of them do not work steadily, but on the whole they work very well.
These Indians should be given more consideration in the matter of housing. I know that a lot of the houses are provided from the welfare fund belonging to the band. These houses are normally all built along the main road, the gravel road, that goes through the reserve. If there is only one road, they are dotted along the side of it. There is not sufficient room on my reserve along that road for all the houses. There are probably well over 1,200 people on the reserve, and they would need about 400 homes. There is no room along the road to build all these houses because there has to be some land connected with the house. There is no point in providing them with a home which is some distance away from the land which has been allotted them. These homes should be provided for them on their land, wherever it is. They
Interim Supply
should be provided with other things, but I do not believe the Indians should expect to have these things provided for nothing. They should work for them and they should have to repay a certain amount for the privilege of having the facilities that are provided.
I notice that my time has almost expired, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to mention that within the last few days I received a letter from the chief of the Six Nations band at Ohsweken, Ontario. He says that the administrators of the Lady Willingdon hospital are charging Indians for hospitalization. I do not understand this, because when Indians are ill in my part of the country they receive free treatment. They claim this as part of the agreement made when they signed the treaty with the Canadian government in the name of Queen Victoria. I should like to quote from the letter:
By explicit assurance, the Six Nations council were informed on May 24, 1956, that the Department of National Health and Welfare would in future cease sending accounts for medical services rendered until arrangements for a health plan were realized.
These people have received bills for hospitalization from the hospital in their district. I hope when the minister or his parliamentary secretary reply to some of the questions that have been asked they will tell us why the Six Nations band is being charged for hospitalization.
There was a news item in the Ottawa Journal for Friday, July 31 from Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, in which it was stated that some 30 Indians were removed from residence in a motel because the accommodation was needed for other people. If there was not a good reason for removing these people from this accommodation, then I say this is a disgrace to Canada. I hope the minister will have the report investigated and tell us exactly what the true story is. The newspaper article refers to the fact the attorney general of Ontario is investigating a case, but since the federal government is responsible for Indian affairs I believe the federal government should investigate the matter. We are entitled to a report on that as well.
I know a great many people on this side of the chamber have a lot of things they wish to say about interim supply. I shall have more to say on other issues, but in the 30 minutes allotted me I cannot say more at this time. Therefore I thank you for allowing me a hearing, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, this motion on interim supply has been before the committee

Interim Supply
since one week ago today and, judging by the remarks of the last speaker, it may be before us all the balance of this week as well. While the members of the official opposition decry the use of the word filibuster, so far this debate has had all the earmarks of a filibuster because the major part of the time for the past week has been taken up by the official opposition. I am not complaining about that; I merely want to point out some facts to see if we can find some solution to the impasse parliament has reached.
It is said that we must scrutinize the $700 million involved in this motion but, as each member of the committee knows, all these matters can be much more appropriately discussed on the estimates when they are called item by item, something which does not happen when an interim supply motion is before us. As a matter of fact, interim supply is usually used to raise major grievances and not to deal with individual departments. It is said that the reason for the long delay is that we are waiting for answers, but of course there have not been questions asked; there has not been any scrutiny during the past week of the different items before the committee. Instead there have been innumerable speeches all of which could equally well have been made on the first item of the estimates of each department.
The feeling one has in listening to this debate is that many of these speeches are being made for the sake of delaying the next item, or the item which will come after we deal with the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, namely the flag debate. I am not saying this in any criticism of the Progressive Conservative members. I am simply seeking to bring out into the light of day what I think is the real malaise in the House of Commons at the present time.
Members of the Progressive Conservative party, at least most of them, feel very honestly and strongly about the flag debate and the flag issue. There are certain things they would like to see in the flag; and while I do not share their views I certainly respect their right to advance their views and to register their opposition. But I think we might as well recognize the fact that the real impasse in the business of the Commons revolves around the flag issue, and if we can find some way of resolving that I am sure the House of Commons could get on with the business which should properly be before it.
As I said before, and I want to repeat very briefly, from the very beginning we in the

New Democratic party have felt that the government was making a mistake in introducing the flag issue at this time. We felt there were many much more important and vital issues before the Canadian people and the House of Commons. We felt that by introducing the flag question the government was very successfully blocking its own legislative program.
On June 3 the Prime Minister announced some 38 items he would like to have disposed of before a summer recess. Only by a great deal of discussion and debate did we finally get an agreement among all parties that there were six items which would have to be dealt with before we returned to the flag debate. It is now apparent that if the debate on interim supply is going to go all of this week, and then the second reading and committee stage of the federal-provincial fiscal relations measure goes on all of next week, followed by the flag debate, the house will be sitting well on into September and will probably carry on to Christmas.
I think we have to try to find a solution. In essence, the government has said "No flag, no recess," and the official opposition is saying no-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member will appreciate that I hesitate very much to interrupt his remarks at this time. I have assumed until now that the references he has made to the flag debate are merely introductory to the substance of the speech he wants to make, but I have some grave reservations as to whether the comments he has made until now are relevant to the resolution before the committee. The hon. member might wish to indicate to the Chair in what way these remarks are related to the resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I shall certainly abide by your ruling, but I am not seeking to debate the flag. The motion on interim supply allows an hon. member to raise any grievance, and I am raising the grievance that the procedures we have adopted for the business of the house are delaying the passage of this motion and are holding up the business of the house. I did not rise for the purpose of arguing about the flag debate but with the idea of bringing forth some possible solution by which we might bring the present debate to a speedy conclusion. I was saying that the government's position is that if there is no flag decision made there will be no recess, and the official opposition is saying

that if there is no recess there will be no money voted, so we are in an impasse.
I suggest that when parliament reaches a stalemate there is only one way to resolve it, and that is for reasonable men to try to find a compromise by which each side will give way to some extent and find a solution. I am not suggesting a compromise because I think it is terribly important that we have a summer recess. I am just as anxious as any other hon. member to get back and spend some time in my constituency, but that is not of paramount importance. I am prepared, as I am sure other hon. members are, to stay here right through to Christmas if it would serve any useful purpose, but I am more concerned about the image which parliament is projecting on the Canadian scene.
I am concerned about the fact that parliament is declining in public esteem. The Canadian people know this country faces very major problems, know that we have on the order paper legislative programs which ought to be dealt with, and dealt with speedily, and they know that parliament is spending its time day after day, and it may be week after week, debating interim supply, and will later be spending still more time debating the flag question.
All of us have to be concerned about what happens to the public image of parliament. We are living in a fast moving age, and people expect parliament to be able to conduct its business with efficiency and dispatch. If the public ever lose faith in our parliamentary institutions, then we shall have done serious damage to democracy itself. Therefore all of us ought to be concerned, and I am sure many of us are, about this decline of parliament in public esteem.
I am not going to go into the question of the need for changes in our rules. We have set up committees for that purpose. What is needed most of all is a change in attitude by which we ourselves accept some measure of self discipline. This means that when we reach an impasse both sides should be willing to give way and reach some compromise that will enable parliament to conduct its business efficiently and effectively.
I say this without casting reflections on any person. I think those who hold strong views against a distinctive national flag do so honestly and sincerely, but I think the government-while it may have been in error when it introduced the flag issue-is with equal sincerity trying to get this matter brought to a head. Therefore I am offering this suggestion as a possible compromise, in the hope
Interim Supply
that the Prime Minister and his supporters and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and his supporters will give some thought to it.
I am suggesting two things; first, that the government be prepared to postpone the flag issue, after the amendment has been voted on, until the fall. I am suggesting that when we come to the flag debate we vote on the amendment which was moved by the official opposition, and then adjourn the debate until we meet some time in the fall.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Why not adjourn it now?

On the other hand, if the government will agree to that, I suggest that the opposition groups agree to an order of the house which would limit the debate on the flag, when it comes up, to a period of one week.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is closure.

There would be no value at all in postponing the flag debate unless when it does come up the time is limited; for if we are going to spend weeks on the flag debate we would be better to spend that time now, in what would normally be a recess, rather than taking up time this fall which ought to be devoted to some very important legislation, including the Canada pension plan, the railway legislation, a national labour code and other things which ought to be dealt with this fall.
And agriculture.

And agriculture, yes. It seems to me this calls for concessions on both sides. The government has said it does not want to leave the flag debate until the fall. I think if they are prepared to give way on that point, we on this side of the house should be equally prepared to give way by agreeing that when the flag debate comes up it will be limited to a stated period of time. I am suggesting one week, but that is a matter, of course, for negotiation among the house leaders.
I make this suggestion, Mr. Chairman, without having any ulterior motive in mind or any sinister purpose. I and my colleagues are prepared to sit here as long as anyone else, but I do not think we are serving any useful purpose, and I certainly do not think we are serving democratic institutions well, if we have weeks of protracted debate simply for the sake of talking. I believe that a compromise could be worked out, if not by the house leaders then by a meeting of the party leaders, in order to get the business of parliament back on the rails, and to see if we

Interim Supply
cannot dispose quickly of this motion and the legislation dealing with federal-provincial relations, deal with the flag in so far as the amendment is concerned, then adjourn until the fall with an understanding that when we come back we will deal with the flag for only a limited period of time.
It seems to me this would partly serve the purposes and desires of both sides of the house. It would mean both would have to give way to some extent, but I think it would commend itself to the Canadian people if they saw parliament back working on important matters rather than appearing to be wasting time frivolously. We in this house do not want to be accused of being governed by childish petulance and wilful stubbornness. I think if we want to avoid that accusation we ought to try to find some common ground on which we could proceed together to do the public business efficiently and effectively.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I naturally have been very interested in the suggestion of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I take it from the reaction of the Acting Prime Minister, who applauded the remarks of the hon. gentleman, that he is in agreement therewith. Indeed, there are in the house at the present time five ministers, at a time when we are discussing some $700 million of expenditures, and the reaction of these gentlemen would seem to indicate that the suggestion made by the hon. member is acceptable to them.
Certainly I am one of those who at all times have believed in the need of compromise in parliament while not sacrificing principle. If, as a result of what has been said by the hon. member-with the evident approval of the ministers opposite, who in applauding must have accepted the suggestion-this suggestion is acceptable, I would be most happy to meet with the Prime Minister at once in this connection.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member has spoken of the image of parliament. Well, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. Today there are those who criticize parliament, who speak of its ineffectiveness and of its wastefulness of time. Those people have always been with us. I was particularly interested in the discussions that took place a week or so ago at the Couchiching conference. I was interested in the views expressed there, and particularly those of Dr. Crick, who recently wrote an

outstanding work on parliament. I have not the summary of it here, but I read it two or three weeks ago when it came out. Those who send to the library and secure that work will learn of the widespread criticism in the United Kingdom. I see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He is a constitutional expert.
Sometimes.

I was interested in the expression of his views the other day, that while there is such a thing as cabinet solidarity that does not apply to parliamentary secretaries, who are required only to agree with the policies of the ministers of their own departments. That is a constitutional position that has no basis in fact and would be a dangerous expedient to be accepted by any parliament.
I am not debating that matter, sir, but I saw the charming countenance of the parliamentary secretary, and as he had been kind enough to give me his views in this connection I thought I would also give him my views in the same spirit of good fellowship that he always exhibits in the house.
Hear, hear.

I have referred to this book. It is of interest to read some of the views expressed therein, for as I deal with them I am also reviewing the Canadian position with regard to parliament. It is the responsibility of members of parliament to examine the expenditures of the government, and that is what is being done.
The hon. member indicates that only important matters, as he put it, should be dealt with. His major contribution in the course of this debate-I say this with the greatest of deference to the hon. member-had to do with the subject of taxis and taxi service at the Toronto airport. I am not criticizing him for dealing with that, but if only matters of transcendent national importance are to be considered at a time when $700 million of estimates are before the house, I would ask him to judge that contribution of his on the basis of his own measurement of this committee.
I have taken it upon myself today, while the debate has been going on, to look up what Mr. Ward, a professor at Saskatchewan university, had by say on the subject of the public purse, and it is very interesting. He says at page 252 of his book entitled "The Public Purse".
The new Auditor General.. .has suggested in his first report how the picture can be made clearer still.

This is in connection with estimates, sup-plementaries, and the like.
Like supplementary estimates, interim supply and governor general's warrants (both of which are explained in preceding chapters) could if improperly used almost destroy parliamentary control. Just as a government could evade unwelcome scrutiny by asking for supplementaries embodying important proposals at a time when parliament was preoccupied with some other weighty matter, or during the hot humid summer days when members are anxious to get away (and both of these events have been known to occur), so a government could time its requests for interim supply in such a manner that the House of Commons would have considerable practical difficulty in refusing. Sir Robert Borden, while prime minister, informed the house of one revealing experience he had had:
-and these are his words:
"I should like to say that I myself tried once, in opposition, under what I thought were somewhat serious circumstances, the policy of refusing any vote on account (that is, interim supply), and before ten days were over, I got very tired of my position, because I heard, I think, from every province and from nearly every community in Canada on the subject".
Then Mr. Ward continues:
Two safeguards protect the Commons, and thus the citizens, from almost all improper uses of interim supply nowadays.. .Interim supply, as W.S. Fielding and Sir Robert Borden agreed in the debate just quoted, can be voluntarily obtained only with the consent of the whole house; a fact which, paradoxically, forced the government in the same debate to impose closure in order to obtain any interim supply at all.
The hon. gentleman has spoken of compromise. In the days when he and I were members of this house before he left for the salubrious atmosphere of Saskatchewan to become the premier of that province there was a spirit of compromise shown by Mr. Mackenzie King. Mr. Ward's book deals with this in these words:
Two clear demonstrations of the house's power over interim supply have been seen in modern times: in 1942, Mr. J. L. Ilsley, while minister of finance in a government supported by a large majority, asserted that interim supply was "wholly within the control of the opposition, not of the government," and reduced a request for interim supply in half, taking one twelfth instead of one sixth, in the face of resistance from the opposition; and in 1956-
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, with that acute memory which he possesses, will recall the pipe line debate of that year.
-as a by-product of the momentous pipe line debate and the subsequent motion of non-confidence in the Speaker in June of that year, the government found itself almost out of funds and at the mercy of the opposition. No one who witnessed that sitting of the house could have any doubts of the power of the weapon which the
Interim Supply
members held, until spokesmen of the various opposition parties made clear that they had chosen to lay it down.
There are further quotations I could place before the committee which clearly indicate the great responsibility resting on members to get information. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has said "Oh, we can wait until the estimates come in". He is certainly filled with optimistic hope in view of the rate of action of this government in bringing forward estimates, a matter I intend to place on record. In this regard it is the worst record in Canadian history. The government has failed to bring the estimates before this house. It is a record which brings about a diminution of respect on the part of people for parliament. The hon. member has said' that the image of parliament diminishes. I sometimes wonder whether the degree to which that trend is apparent is the result of managed news or managed information regarding parliament, but I will deal with that on another occasion.
Parliament can never be effective unless full information on its activities is available. Parliament can never be effective if what goes over the airways and what appears on television is selective information. I emphasize that because I am sure the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, one of the fine exponents of television art, will concur with that view. Indeed, I am not here to be flattering, but I always listen to him on television because he displays that same graciousness which he always shows in this house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I had better leave.

No, don't go away. Perhaps the hon. gentleman finds himself too close to the Minister of Justice, who himself has not in his period of time shown the same regard for parliament as the parliamentary secretary who sat beside him a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member does not like sitting next to me because I can see his blushes.

There is no danger of the Minister of Justice blushing over compliments about the way he has been carrying on. Of course I also say of him that he is gracious no matter how arbitrary he may be.
Dr. Crick whom I mentioned a moment ago went on to say:
By comparison with the popular assembly of almost any other free country, parliament has fallen hideously behind the times both in its procedures and in the facilities that it extends to its members, and there is good ground for thinking

Interim Supply
that it would benefit from some fairly drastic internal alterations and repairs which would go far beyond mere patching. Despite the general complacency of M.P.'s themselves, there has been evidence lately of public concern: flare-ups of indignation and mockery in the popular press, worried soul searchings and reassurances in the heavier papers.
I am not going to mention that we have had similar experiences, nor endeavour to define which of the Canadian papers would qualify as the heavier ones. He continues:
Parliamentary reform has actually become a newsworthy topic. Some M.P.'s are aware of a growing scepticism, even hostility, certainly bewilderment, among the public; but the house as a whole seems to react only by an increasing touchiness about "privilege"-
This indicates that the same criticism we have, and it is healthy that there should be criticism, is taking place in the United Kingdom.
While the rules in the United Kingdom, as here, are not as immutable as the laws of the Medes and Persians they are subject to change: parliaments are loathe to change the rules. I am speaking of the British parliament, which was good enough to assure the survival of freedom through two world wars.
The author then deals with the levels of confusion in the public's mind and says:
Parliament is to be seen as a form of publicity- its real functions are those of alerting and informing the public on matters relevant to the decision which way (or whether) to vote.
The power of parliament lies in its means and right to control the cabinet in respect of expenditures it makes, and to ensure that the imposition of taxation shall be carefully examined and scrutinized; because governments, even though they are minority governments, become arrogant. They do not like to be examined, and they do not like to answer questions. I am going to refer to the number of questions that have been asked during the last week and then point out the fact that we have not been able to get any answers. I do not know where the ministers are.
Europe.

There has been an indication in answers to questions that one has sought the sweetening climate of Capri. While parliament sits he suns. When questions are asked he is not here to answer them. It is a strange development that is taking place among the ministers opposite. We saw the beginning of this during the debate on the defence bill, when the minister of defence refused to answer the questions of the opposition, or simply disdained to answer. We have seen this attitude on several subsequent

occasions. Only Friday I asked the Prime Minister whether the Minister of Agriculture was speaking for the government when he announced in Prince Edward Island that loan legislation would be brought in in order to permit groups of farmers to buy farm machinery under the best possible circumstances for them. The name of the legislation was given by the minister outside the House of Commons. The Prime Minister said, apparently not knowing what the Minister of Agriculture had said, that an announcement of policy will be made in the house.
This attitude has been held in respect of various departments, and it continued during the past week. How many questions were asked last week? The computer shows the number of questions asked on Monday as 148, on Tuesday 32, on Wednesday 3, on Thursday 12 and on Friday 37, a total of 232. How many answers have we received? We have not received one answer, and have not seen any endeavour made to answer the questions. The hon. member for Vegreville has asked, about $700 million? It has been suggested that we wait until later on when the estimates come in, at which time we will be given further information. We actually have not even been told that, and I should like to know the reason.
The first principle that is enunciated by every parliamentary authority is that governments shall answer questions during the debate on interim supply. Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure and Practice in the Dominion of Canada-and I use the word "dominion" advisedly even though some would establish a republic here and do not like the word-states as follows:
One of the principal purposes of the House of Commons is the consideration and criticism of the estimates and the taxes required to meet the public expenditure; and the committees of supply and ways and means are the parliamentary machinery through which the house chiefly exercises these political and constitutional functions.
Durell says the chief functions of the House of Commons "-are to criticize, discuss and amend, and finally approve or disapprove of the policy of the government as laid before it". In order to carry out this function it is necessary that members are given full information and freedom to discuss various issues. We are asking for information. I say to you, sir, there is no filibuster in the demand of the opposition for its constitutional right to have information from the government, which sits there, if it is present at all, silent and contemptuous.
Hear, hear.

The bedrock on which the parliamentary system is built is the maintenance by parliament of control over the grants which it makes. Durell has summed that up in these words:
-the House of Commons should control the finance of the country...It has been achieved by means of struggles lasting through centuries, beginning from the fourteenth century down to the seventeenth century, when it was fully confirmed and since then it has never been practically disputed.
It has not been disputed, but it has been arrogantly flouted by this government which has refused to answer questions. I intend to place before this house some of the questions that have been asked in respect of which answers and information have been refused. I realize that the committee of supply, which is the chief apparatus through which the House of Commons makes effective its absolute control over the expenditures of government, is not the most effective body. The hon. member mentioned the fact that speeches are made by members. That is true. It is not the most effective body but through the generations it has proven to be the best there is in that connection.
However, there are some who suggest that greater attention should be given to committees in parliament. It is of interest that on Friday last the house leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition asked this question with regard to the business of the house:
Will the government, In response to the many requests made from this side of the house, refer three or four departments of estimates to special or standing committees?
Sir, why will they not do so? Are they afraid they will have to answer if these estimates go before committees? Is that why they go ahead in the house behind a smokescreen?
They want to charge the opposition with obstruction.

What is the reason? The reason they are not answering questions is simply that they want to lead the people to believe that the opposition is frustrating them. That is what they are trying to do. The only frustration to parliament consists in hon. gentlemen sitting opposite who apparently do not want to answer. Certainly they have not answered. Is it because they do not know the answers? In all the years I have been in the house I have never known any government which has refused any 20220-399
Interim Supply
answers to parliament to the same extent. Never before has this happened. What are they trying to do? Was not the first question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre a reasonable one? Certainly some departments have been sent to committees. The Department of External Affairs-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the only one.

That is the only one. Are they trying to have an examination made? Last Tuesday one of the members of the press gallery said that the opposition was engaged in a filibuster. That is what he said on Tuesday, one day after the discussion got under way. He has been backtracking ever since. Finally he came out and said: There will be no more trouble in this connection because there is division in the opposition, or the Leader of the Opposition is going to change his attitude. I have no attitude except to see that parliament works as parliament should work, rather than being frustrated by a government which would emasculate this institution for its own purposes.
This was the next question asked by the house leader of the official opposition:
Will the government give an undertaking to the house that for the remainder of this session at least two full days a week will be set aside for a discussion of the main estimates, as has been the practice in other sessions?
I am going to place on the record what has been the practice. Just imagine. On the 118th day of the session the government has not brought a main estimate before the house. What manner of subterfuge is this on the part of the government? What are they hiding? What are they concealing? The next question was:
If neither of these plans is followed, will the government let us know when during this session the main estimates are to be considered and how much time will be made available for that purpose?
What was the answer? The new Minister of National Revenue as acting house leader stated that he could not answer because consultation was necessary. What is the reason for this? Is this a campaign of silence? Give us the answers. Give us replies to the questions asked before you ask the House of Commons to say to you that for the next two months you have got $700 million to do with what you like. I cannot say to the government house leader, what happened in the past, because he was not here; but I ask other ministers with experience: Why do you do this to parliament?

Interim, Supply
I listen to the so-called objective observations that are broadcast over radio and television. Some of them, so far as spontaneity is concerned, appear to be inspired by the government of the country. Sir, on Friday 23 questions were asked the ministers and 18 suggestions, recommendations or charges were made, but not an answer was given. What is the reason?
Up to the present time I have quoted textbook authorities. I shall quote one more and then I will quote the present Prime Minister. Mr. Bourinot in his book entitled Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, has this to say on page 423:
On going into committee of supply or ways and means it is the practice for members to ask questions of the government, but when a minister has replied it is not regular for him to speak again until a new question is proposed from the Chair...
If we waited until replies were received there would just be the question and then there would be a vote. Why this conspiracy of silence? Why this attempt on the part of the government to hide the facts from the Canadian people? Many commentators I have read are saying it is common to pass interim supply perfunctorily. That was not the view of hon. gentlemen sitting opposite in 1962. They took seven days on $300 million. Were the parliamentary rules not in effect in December, 1962? What did the Prime Minister say at that time?
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made. When these rights are ignored-
You can just hear him as he emphasized each of those words.
Mr. Chairman-
No, not now.
-would the right hon. gentleman give the page reference?

I beg your pardon. It is page 2834. I am sorry I am not able to quote the hon. gentleman in this connection because he remained silent during those days. The Prime Minister went on to say:
When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament itself is being violated and we are taking a step toward its destruction.
Seven days for $300 million.
Mr. Chairman, I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, acting as prime minister, and to the government: Physician, heal thyself. When parliament does not get information it is violated.
I wonder whether the right hon. gentleman would permit a question on the quotation he has made-
Surely.

-in which he quoted the words "these rights are being violated". Would he agree with me that the rights that were being discussed then concerned the right of parliament to have a budget brought before it for examination?

The hon. gentleman has earned the applause of those who sit around him because they do not realize that he was as close to the facts in that question as he usually is. Here are the words:
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made.
This is what he was talking about, and then he said:
When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament itself is being violated-
Then, we find these words:
No matter how wide a circulation we give and no matter in what form, to the bill of rights, and no matter how much we may talk about Magna Carta and the bill of rights, no matter how emotionally we may wrap ourselves up in parliamentary or national flags-
Those are pertinent words, "no matter how emotionally we may wrap ourselves up in parliamentary or national flags"-
-both these rights I have mentioned are being deliberately and systematically violated by the present government.
I never knew before I would be able to pay such tribute to the Prime Minister's vast power to look ahead because, as the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam has said, the flag question plays a large part in the Prime Minister's plan for the people of Canada. Yet at the same time, on the order paper, there are a great many matters that deserve attention and which have been shoved aside. The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot-hon. gentlemen on the other side laugh. Their contribution in that corner has never been greater than the depth and importance of their laughter.
These hon. gentlemen pointed out the serious situation of agriculture in the province of Quebec and in eastern Canada. What is the answer?
Let them eat cake.
They answer with silence; there has been no answer.
Watching closely.

Why emphasize one matter at the expense of the others? Look at these matters on the order paper which are not going to be dealt with, and yet there was no reference to the flag in the speech from the throne. Rome was not built in a day, but a flag was planned for Canadian people in a rush in nine days. Why this haste? Everything is being shoved aside, and parliament and its functions are being circumscribed. Parliament has ceased to be an instrument whereby the opposition can secure information simply because the Prime Minister and those associated with him want to bring about something that will not improve the economic conditions of Canadians today and will not meet the problems that have been brought before this house in the last week or during this session.
It is a serious commentary on a government that is trying, with those who give it their support, to lead the Canadian people into believing the opposition is holding things up. I spoke on the opening day of interim supply. I dealt with a serious situation in connection with the board of trustees. I asked questions that Canadians had a right to have answered. There was not one answer, not one word. I asked for an opportunity to examine these trustees in a committee of parliament. There was not one answer, just uncertainty. Here we have $700 million in expenditures which we cannot hope to examine in detail. We have the right to ask for redress of the things we say are wrong. The Minister of Veterans Affairs is not here today, but veterans affairs have been mentioned. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was asked questions in connection with the serious derogation of rights of individuals.
What about the questions asked by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories and the plans to save millions for Canadian taxpayers? What about questions asked by one hon. member after another? Is this what you call parliament? The government sits-I am not going to say "thinks"-the government sits and, yes, thinks it is going to get away with this. I want to thank the hon. member for Wellington South for furnishing me with a survey of the sessions 1955-56; 1959-60 and 1960-61, all of them non-election years. This survey indicates the time required to deal with the main estimates amounts to 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the total number of sitting days. We have not had these estimates as yet. For what reason are they kept back? All the government does is say to us, 20220-399J
Interim Supply
"gimme, gimme, gimme", in advance. It will not bring in these main estimates.
That was the record in the past. In so far as this session is concerned, 15 departments have been called and 2 have been completed, agriculture and post office. The estimates of external affairs have been transferred to the standing committee on external affairs. The estimates of public works have been before the committee for one day. There are 11 other departments that have been available for consideration since the supply motions of April 21, May 5 and May 26. Six more departments will be called after two more supply motions have been called. The departments that have been called so far are citizenship and immigration, labour, northern affairs and national resources, and industry. I should like to look into that department. All one has to do is to look at the answer given today to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, to see what is happening under this government. There has been a multiplication of positions. It used to be said that rabbits multiply, but rabbits have nothing on this government.
Appointments made as a result of competitions organized by the civil service commission from May 1, 1963 to May 31, 1964 numbered 18,201. What manner of thing is this? These are appointments as a result of competitions and we have a multiplication of bureaucracy. Questions are asked and no answers are given, except today. This answer indicates there were 299 appointments in the Department of Forestry. Where is the Minister of Forestry?
Capri.
I have often heard romantic songs refer to that place.
Mr. Chairman, I can answer the question as to where the Minister of Forestry is.
I am always glad to have answers from the hon. minister.

The Minister of Forestry has been attending an international conference on forestry affairs, along with the corresponding ministers of 32 other nations, in Italy. The other countries invited were: Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Jordan, Libya, Lebanon, Luxembourg, Morocco, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Rumania, Spain, Syria, Sweden, Switzerland, Tunisia, Turkey, United Arab

Interim Supply
Republic, United Kingdom, the U.S.A. and Yugoslavia.

The impossible has been achieved; an answer has been secured. Today the dominion bureau of statistics reports federal employment increased by 4,032 over March 1963. That increase was as follows: national defence, 2,181, post office 2,368, national revenue, income tax branch 2,652-I thought when we were in office we had enough income tax officers and officials-public works 414, secretary of state 135-I would think they had enough in that department before they started to increase the number-trade and commerce, bureau of statistics branch, 629.
This is the government which says it has solved unemployment. There are a few less unemployed than when we were in office, but they do not refer to that any more. The unemployment insurance commission increased by 1,517. I wonder what they are doing. What was the reason for the increase? When I mention increases I point out that is the number appointed as a result of competitions, and no doubt there have been some withdrawals. Sir, nothing else has been achieved. Now we have got an answer from the minister. It was the first time he has ever been able to answer a question but he was fortified by the civil service providing him with that list of countries.
During this session only eight days have been allotted for main estimates, that is, only one third to one half the time normally given to main estimates during the first 110 days of a session. Then they ask why we ask questions. Just imagine that. Sir, parliament operates in co-operation, but if one side says, "We are just going to let the opposition ferret things out on their own; we are not going to answer any questions" then parliament becomes a hollow shell. It becomes a caricature of its responsibilities, and that is what is happening. We ask for these answers, and we will ask for these answers. I make that formal request now, that the ministers who are absent, either with or without leave, answer the questions asked. I have a list of questions which I will put on the record on a later occasion when I speak again, if necessary. I told you the number that has been asked and of all the hundreds of questions that have been asked one has been answered.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: How many days did that conference last?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It was an incomplete answer.

We will have to have the minister tell us how many days this conference will last. Possibly he will have this information and I shall sit down immediately to enable him to furnish it. What are the dates on which the conference is held? When did the minister leave and when will he return? These are simple questions that the President of the Privy Council should have no difficulty answering. Is the minister now ready to depart from the customary manner adopted by the government and tell us how many days was the conference?

No, Mr. Chairman, I am not ready to depart from the customary procedure. If the Leader of the Opposition wants this information it can be obtained for him and put on the record in the proper way. That will be done. I can tell him that the main part of the conference lasted for three days, and I will get, and give him the rest of the information.
According to my computations he has been gone a longer while than the time to allow him to get over there and back. Where is he now?
Capri.
The minister expressed his view that if he were to rise to answer questions he would be departing from the rules of parliament. Isn't that a new one?
No, I did not say that. The right hon. gentleman ought not to misquote.

Mr. Chairman, one cannot misquote anything that has never been said. Well, I declare. "Don't misquote" said the minister. I wanted him to give the information and then he says, "Put it on the order paper and we will answer it". What a record that is. We had an example of it today. The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm asked a question. He asked it as a starred question on February 25, five and a half months ago. Then the government brings it along today and passes it as an order for return. A lot more questions will be referred to that have not been answered.
We asked the government to give the answers to the questions we have asked. Questions asked by members of the Social Credit party have received no answer. I see I now have the support of one member from that party. It is not holding up parliament to demand information.
What are they concealing? What are they hiding? What about the labour department? What about Banks? There was a short answer

given about Banks. They do not know to the same extent where he is as they do the Minister of Forestry. What of these trustees? They are going to decide whether they are going to appear before parliament.
All of this adds up simply to one fact, that this government has something to hide. It does not want the Canadian people to have the information we have requested. Somebody has to take the responsibility of an opposition to ask these questions. The only answer is the echo of filibuster. Was there a filibuster on the part of the Liberal party in December 1962 when it took eight days on $300 million? When is a filibuster a filibuster? Apparently when a Liberal is in the government position but not when he is in opposition.
I come back, sir, to the point where I started, by saying we are not trying to hold them up. We are trying to get them to give parliament information. I hope for once it will be reported to the Canadian people, the hundreds of questions that have been asked, and the answers given to only two.
Sir, I am not going into particulars as to questions asked, but I am asking this government to give the house answers to these questions between now and Wednesday. They are not going to get away with a policy of hiding, of concealment, of unaccustomed taciturnity. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is a man who has a capacity for language, and I am sure that if we asked him these questions we would have some answers, even though-I am sure he will take this in the kindest spirit-only a person with a dictionary knowledge and a capacity for imagination would be able to actually ascertain the answer when he had spoken.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: To answer questions.

-reply in kind to my right hon. friend. I can well understand the satisfaction that he gets out of the kind of debating effort in which he has just indulged. I have done the same thing on some occasions myself when speaking from that side of the chamber. I can very well understand the psychological impulses, and other impulses, that cause a man to speak for such a long time without really saying too much.

Hear, hear.
Interim Supply

I say that to my right hon. friend in the generous spirit in which a few moments ago he addressed himself to me. He and I do not agree on many things, but we have a certain empathy which allows us to understand why it is not possible for us to have full agreement. But he did ask one question, Mr. Chairman, and I simply want to say, in giving him the reply, that there were 1,684 questions on the order paper, out of which some 1,554 have been answered. That is almost 92 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is more than 92 per cent.
I believe that constitutes a record. Of the 130 remaining, 80 have been put on the order paper since as late as July 20.
How many since April?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have not made that calculation, but I will be very glad to make it for my right hon. friend. But what I rose to do, Mr. Chairman, was not to endeavour to reply to the right hon. gentleman in all of the particulars which he mentioned, but to say to him that we have before us a suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. It was, I am sure, a constructive suggestion and one that was put forward by that hon. gentleman because he feels that parliament must get on with the business before it.
It would be possible for me to offer arguments in answer to my right hon. friend. I could refer him to speeches that have been made on both sides since I have been in this house and since he has been in this house. But at the present time the mood of the nation does not lend itself to an encouragement of this kind of activity in the house.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
While I do not believe that every public criticism of the manoeuvring that goes on in parliament is always justifiable, I do believe that at this time all of us on the government side, the official opposition and the other parties, have a responsibility to the very institution of parliament itself, which responsibility we should face. It was because the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam felt this was the case that he put forward a suggestion that might enable us, without in any way interfering with obligations in opposition, to proceed with the public business with greater dispatch. The hon. gentleman has made a suggestion. I will see that suggestion is brought

Interim Supply
to the attention of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has been engaged in public business in his own constituency today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are going to carry it back to the Prime Minister.

When he returns tonight I will see that this suggestion is put before him. I will also call the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that, while my right hon. friend did not in any way respond to the suggestion-
He did.

-he did say he
would meet with the Prime Minister at the earliest moment.
That is a response.
That is a response, but that is not a direct reply to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
Is the hon. gentleman making a direct reply now?

I am not saying that the right hon. gentleman had an obligation to make an immediate response; I am simply saying the only response he did make was that he would be happy to meet with the Prime Minister on this matter. But I did notice that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre-
He hasn't spoken.

-did not accept for his party the suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. As far as those of us on this side are concerned, including myself, I applauded the hon. gentleman for Burnaby-Coquitlam because I thought he made honestly a constructive suggestion.
Will you accept it now?
Mr. Chairman, my right hon. friend asks if I will accept it. I would want to give it consideration-
Oh, oh.

-as my right hon. friend would expect, because the Prime Minister of the country is out of the house at the moment. But this matter will be brought to his attention. This worthy suggestion is one that will be carefully considered not only by the Prime Minister but by his colleagues in the government. That is what a suggestion of
(Mr. Martin (Essex East).]
that kind warrants and merits, and will receive.
What I do say to the right hon. gentleman is this. I could indulge now in debate with him point for point with regard to the various points he has raised; but this would settle nothing. It would satisfy the debating instincts of the right hon. gentleman and myself, but it would not satisfy the Canadian people at this time.
Hear, hear.

No one denies that the opposition has the responsibility to examine the expenditures proposed by the government. No one denies that the granting of interim supply lies, in the final analysis, with the opposition. No one denies the right of the opposition to scrutinize to the hilt every proposed expenditure-
And to get information.

-that is put forward by the government. No one denies that, and that is not in issue. My right hon. friend does injustice to parliament itself when he suggests there is any contrary view. But I do say to my right hon. friend seriously that he is an officer of this house, and when parliament is attacked within and without, those of us who have been in this house for a long time, who treasure this institution and who have made our contribution to it according to our talents, must not in any way unwittingly be parties to the process of destruction that is going on.
Remember your dates.

I said at the outset that I remember sitting where my right hon. friend is sitting, or close by, and doing what I could to criticize the government of which he was the head. I played my part in the attack, but the records of this house will show, I think, that there were at least limits, and I suggest that we have reached those limits now.
There were no limits.

My right hon. friend says there were no limits, but I would put to him this. The test of statesmanship is not to give tit for tat, not to say: "Because you did this we are going to do it". I would say to my right hon. friend now, let us acknowledge that we have had a worth-while suggestion made, a suggestion that we should carefully consider. Let us examine that suggestion on its merits not because we have in our memories the shades

of events in the past. Let us devote ourselves now to the public business. If we do that we will find that our political interests will not suffer. The political interests of the government or of the opposition groups will not suffer because a few less speeches are made. I urge that we examine this proposal. We on this side will certainly examine it. I know the Prime Minister will be desirous of giving it very careful consideration. I would invite my right hon. friend, who has-I hope he has- the authority for directing the course of the official opposition, to give now the kind of leadership, along with the leadership which the Prime Minister of this country will give, which would assist us in getting down to the public business, and showing the nation that this institution of parliament is destined to continue and flourish in its present form for a long time, an institution which must continue because it is the guarantor of the liberties we cherish.

Mr. Chairman, it is noticeable that none applaud that peroration more than some who sit opposite and who destroyed parliament during the pipe line debate by their contempt for parliament. Naturally they applaud today the pontifical statements of the hon. gentleman; but he did fail to do one thing. He failed to remove all the underbrush. Ask yourself this question, Mr. Chairman: Did he say that we were going to get answers to the 232 or more questions which we asked last week and which up to the present time have been contemptuously disregarded by ministers, most of whom are absent?

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question of the secretary of state. I should like to ask him whether, in view of the remarks he has just made, he would recommend to the leader of his party that he withdraw the two flag resolution?
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend knows that the answer to that is clearly, no.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee was suitably touched by the sweet reasonableness of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I am wondering just on what premise he could stand up in this committee and say the things which he did. He now says that, now that the Liberals are in government let everybody be sweetly reasonable and make sure that we go ahead so that the Liberals can remain in power. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was the man who when in opposition said: "Any
Interim Supply
means we shall use to bring down this government". We remember those words. Any tactics were justified when the Liberals were in opposition. But now they are in government parliament must reform and put such matters aside. Were those tactics reprehensible in the hands of the Liberal opposition if today hon. gentlemen opposite say they are reprehensible in the hands of the present opposition? However I will not indulge in any long exchange in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, we have reached the 118th day of this session. The past week has been used in the study of the estimates of certain departments on a cohesive, logical basis. Speeches were made by members of the opposition-and an opportunity also existed for government members-which would have been made on the first item of those departments. The reason is quite clear, and I do not intend to repeat the statistics quoted by the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam conveniently glossed over the performance in December, 1962, and prior to his entry into this parliament the performance of some of the more experienced members opposite, in the consideration of supplementary estimates and interim supply during the period when the Liberals were in opposition. I know we hear shouts of "filibuster", and that sort of thing, but they are from members whose experience here dates from last year and whose contributions have been even shorter.
I have found a lack of logic on the part of certain commentators and editorial writers who ask-I believe this was also raised at the Couchiching conference-what is the role of the backbencher; and then we see those thunderous ukases on the editorial pages to the effect that the backbencher is nothing but a tame individual subject to the party whip and that instead he should assert his independence; that if he fails to agree with the party stand he should stand up and say so. In the so-called spirit of the words of the hon. member for Northumberland, he should disagree. Well, Mr. Chairman, how does one disagree but by speaking and expressing his point of view?
On the other hand these selfsame editorial writers and others are saying that parliament must get on with the dispatch of the public's business, and get on with it at a most amazing speed. I notice that some editorial writers feel that if they agree with government policy, then further discussion is unnecessary; that as long as you are on the side of the majority then opposition to that majority is negligible and should be stifled; that as long as one

Interim Supply
agrees that anyone who disagrees must not be heard at length, this is acceptable.
I am touched by the stand taken in certain newspapers which suggest we have now spoken, should cease this discussion, vote and get on to something else. These people are not here. They like to use high sounding phrases which they polish in their ivory towers. I should like to see some of them come here and acquire some knowledge about this institution. I disagree entirely with these people who spend their time denigrating this institution. Certainly it has its faults: We are human beings.
There certainly is a logical process in criticism. One may diagnose and as a result of the diagnosis identify a disease, but unless he prescribes for the disease all he has done is engage in some philosophical exercise. Nowhere do we see any concrete suggestions, which we would undoubtedly welcome. After all, this house is not composed of perfect mortals. I believe a realization of the purpose of this chamber and its organization, as in respect of any democratic system, will show that there can be delays. The delays certainly are not as bad as they are made out to be.
I should like to see a great deal more emphasis placed on those things this parliamentary system has contributed to the good of the country rather than on isolated instances where mistakes have been made. Let us emphasize that which has been done right, for a change, rather than those few wrongs that exist. I am not trying to curb the right of criticism but I think one must be constructively critical.
I suggest the proposal of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in regard to the discussion that is now taking place is inaccurate, and I cannot accept his premise that I am participating in this debate in an attempt to postpone something else. I should like to discuss the estimates of certain departments and have not had an opportunity to do so. I should like to discuss these estimates, in the same way as some members who are not present in this chamber today discussed items before granting supply and continued to discuss them until they were satisfied.
I should like to refer to the former member for Laurier, who has departed this chamber, and who on many occasions asserted that he had something to say and intended to say it. This is the right and purpose of an elected member to this house. I feel certain that any reasonable man who will think about this suggestion will agree with me.
I have repeated on many occasions that a simpler procedure in dealing with these

estimates is to send them to various committees for study. Many of the standing committees were organized late in the session. I feel they were organized at a snail's pace and a good many of them are merely window dressing. These committees do exist on paper but have not met to do any work. Certainly it would have been easy to send the estimates to them for consideration. The estimates of at least two or three departments might now have been studied by the estimates committee.
Some members complain about a conflict in attendance at committee meetings and that members have been named to too many committees. I quite honestly feel that our committees as organized have too many members, thus making them unwieldy. Why should a standing committee have 45 to 60 members? I do not feel these committees should have more than 15 members. We know the difficulties involved in a fully or well attended committee when each member has the right to speak and ask questions. How many questions can a member ask with cohesion during a two to four hours committee meeting? I think it would be much better to have 10, 15 or 20 members dealing with an examination of the estimates in an intelligent manner than to approach this examination from the point of view of using a blunderbuss or a doublebarrelled shotgun.
I am sure my experience indicates that we have had two or three times as much information in respect of these estimates in past years. I think one has only to consider the information provided in November of 1963, which of course was a difficult year when we sat from May until the end of December. In December the hopper was filled with main estimates in an attempt to complete our consideration before Christmas. Great pressure was brought to bear and many of the estimates of the departments received only cursory examination. No wonder these estimates were examined in detail at the first opportunity this spring, at which time opposition members were doing nothing less than that which would be done by hon. members opposite when they sat on this side of the chamber. However these youngsters who spend their time as gad-flies continue to shout "filibuster". I suggest that is utter nonsense. I think these members are doing a disservice by acting in this way.
I am well aware of the attitude taken by the more serious minded members on the opposite side when they were in opposition. That attitude was more constructive in the consideration of estimates. For the benefit of

those who have not sat in opposition I should point out that the feeling in 1958 was that government backbenchers had to learn their lessons by bitter experience. Many hon. members opposite do not subscribe to the theory of infallibility, yet their attitude is that because these expenditures are listed in the blue estimates book they are correct. When the chairman calls an item it is sacrosanct, and seven or eight members shout "carried, carried, carried". I suggest they are nothing but parrots on a perch.
I must say I find it difficult to accept the suggestion that the purpose and role of a member of parliament is that expressed byindividuals who should come here and learn a great deal more about this system. It is very easy to criticize glibly.
We can always run our neighbours' affairs better than we can our own. But let us be a little more humble about it.
Look at what we are doing. Under these circumstances we have been asked to grant further supply to the government. But the government has not been prepared to give answers. I have never heard of an instance of interim supply when there was not one minister prepared to answer. The opposition today is no less competent than the opposition of yesteryear and in those days those members put forward various meritorious points that were worthy of consideration. It is no less so today. I am sure I could get the Minister of Transport to nod his head violently in agreement on that point because when he was in opposition he certainly felt that any criticisms he made or any inquiries he directed were worthy of consideration and that any speeches he made on interim supply were worthy of consideration.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Yes.

The hon. gentleman chose to refer to me and I should like to ask him this question. Does he not recall that, except for the occasion at the time we were in opposition when supply was asked for the tenth month and it was mathematically certain the estimates would never be brought before the house, we did not hold up interim supply at all? '
This I disagree with.
Look at the facts.

All right, the hon. gentleman says they did not. We know what happened in 1962 in connection with estimates. We know
Interim Supply
what was discussed under the circumstances. The Liberal platform for the forthcoming election was primarily discussed, as it was in 1962 at the time of the supplementary estimates.
We are talking about interim supply.
It was discussed on interim supply. The hon. gentleman and I disagree. I do not agree with him so let us indicate that we have agreed to disagree.
How about the facts?

The hon. gentleman has stated his version of the facts and mine is different. Therefore we disagree.
Having said these things, I wish to turn to a particular department which unfortunately we cannot say should have been sent to a committee, because the government in its choice of the departments to be called has not yet called the Department of Veterans Affairs. This is unfortunate because I think that department should have been called and its estimates sent to the committee. The estimates were considered by the committee last year.
Under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Renfrew North we had a very useful examination of the policies and problems of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Since that time new issues have arisen and I am sure that in a relatively short time we could have had an appropriate discussion and exposure of these problems. We must never forget that until 1958 the discussion of veterans affairs was always a hit or miss proposition, subject to the bringing forward of a special resolution by the government to set up a special committee. Until 1958 it was not one of the standing committees of the house. It was a part of the 1957 platform of the Progressive Conservative party that veterans affairs would be made a matter of study by a standing committee of the house. This was implemented.
We remember that on March 16, a memorable day also because it was budget day, the Minister of Veterans Affairs chose to make a statement with regard to the government's policy concerning veterans hospitals and the relationship of those hospitals with municipal and provincial hospital authorities. There has been discussion with regard to that matter. On a motion to go into supply moved on April 20 the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre moved an amendment in the following terms:
