This house deplores the announced decision of the government to abandon its responsibilities for the administration of veterans hospitals by assigning and transferring certain veterans hospitals to provincial or municipal control, and further deplores the failure of the government to accept the request of the Royal Canadian Legion and other national veterans organizations that the administration and control of the veterans hospitals remain with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
There followed a debate and the amendment was negatived. I do not wish to resurrect that debate, Mr. Chairman, because there was a decision of the house, but since that time when the question of veterans hospitals in this country was very much to the fore the matter has died down. But I do not think the problem has disappeared at all. I am sorry the Minister of Veterans Affairs is not present although I am glad to see his parliamentary secretary here.
What has happened in the interval in regard to this matter? I am very mindful of the recommendation last year of the veterans affairs committee that this whole question be discussed again before the committee, with the national veterans organizations, before the government came to a decision. The government obviously has not accepted that recommendation because it is in the process of coming to a decision. It made a statement through the mouth of the minister. Even though members of the veterans organizations were sitting in the gallery and due to see the minister later that afternoon, a decision was announced prior to the interview.
What has happened in the interval? We would like to get confirmation from the minister or from the government with respect to the situation in Calgary because Calgary seemed to be the most sensitive point. There had been a demand that Colonel Belcher hospital be turned over to the municipal hospital authorities under some proposition involving the province. I gather that this has now been abandoned. What about Edmonton? What is the state of negotiations with regard to the provision of chronic and domiciliary care? We see various snippets in the newspapers with regard to this matter, but just what is to happen? Even if we are told that no decision has been reached, at least there must be an indication with regard to the situation, but there has been an infernal silence with regard to the matter.
What about other centres? What about Sun-nybrook in Toronto? I understand that portions of the pavilions there have had civilian patients placed in them. To what extent has this been done and how is it working out? I think we are entitled to know this

before the whole system is committed. What about Ste. Anne de Bellevue? Are plans going forward for the replacement of those really outworn facilities? We all recognize they are inadequate. Just what has happened in this regard? There was a high intensity of interest last March and April when the government's decision was announced involving a change in policy. After all, the recommendations of the Glassco commission are very much before us. Where are we going? Many thousands of dollars, being one sixth of the annual budget for treatment services, are now in issue before the house.
I think the parliamentary secretary will recognize that we would not have to be talking and asking these questions in the house if the veterans affairs committee had been allowed to discuss these matters with the minister or his parliamentary secretary or the director of treatment services. Dr. Crawford has always been the most co-operative of witnesses. He has always been very helpful and most patient in listening to the points put forward by hon. members on both sides of the house who have an interest in veterans affairs. I am no professional veteran but, like so many other members who were of the right age at the right time, I saw service in our country's forces. We have an interest in our comrades in arms and in what facilities are provided for them.
After all, under the legislation we have on our books we say to a veteran, if you have a pensionable entitlement you are entitled to get service as quickly as possible. We have provided hospitals and we have provided staffs, good staffs. At this point I should like to say I do not agree with some of the implications in the minister's statement of March 16. I absolutely repudiate them. I must say that as his immediate predecessor I found these words passing strange coming from his mouth. This is my first opportunity of saying so. I feel those words would have been better left unsaid because I do not believe our veterans hospitals are approaching any state at the present of what was implied.
Be that as it may, our servicemen and women who have a pensionable entitlement are told, by law, they have certain rights. We cannot disturb those rights by placing these hospitals under municipal authority without ensuring that those rights will not be infringed upon. We know that at the moment there is tremendous pressure on all hospitals from the general public. In some areas you almost have to be an emergency

case before you can be admitted. The veteran is not an emergency case. The law says he does not have to be an emergency case to be admitted to hospital.
There is a provision also under the Pension Act for the veteran who wishes to be treated for a non-pensionable illness in a veterans hospital. You may say he has an advantage because he can gain admission if he has appendicitis or some other illness. If he were to wait on the general, public list, he would have to wait until the cows come home, literally. This is just a part of the general situation that faces us in connection with our general hospitals. However, under the provisions of the act, the veteran has been given the right to be admitted to a veterans hospital and to pay for it himself. Are we going to take that right away from him? The law has been in existence for a long time. This is one of those things the country has said it is going to give to the veteran because he offered his services. I feel it is a small recompense. Why try to get out of that by the back door?
I have not a closed mind in connection with the administration of hospitals in conjunction with municipal authority. In certain areas it has worked out very well. In so far as general administration and housekeeping are concerned, as well as affiliation with a teaching hospital such as the University of Alberta, I think the set-up at the Colonel Mewburn hospital does provide a fine framework within which the proper treatment of our veterans can be given. However, sometimes on week ends there is difficulty with admissions because people are absent on week ends. However, I believe that can be gotten around.
I do feel, Mr. Chairman, that we must get a report at the earliest opportunity from the Minister of Veterans Affairs in regard to this hospital situation. Frankly, I felt the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam was being naive this afternoon, with all due respect to him, when he said we will be able to discuss these things on the main estimates. When will that be-in December? We have to have two more supply motions before we get some of these departments before us. Has there been any indication when we are going to have these supply motions? Perhaps we will get them next November and these departments will be open to us in December. What chance will we have to discuss them at that time?
Negotiations on the hospitals will take place during the next five or six months. I think 20220-400J

There are some things in connection with the Department of Justice upon which I should like to comment, and that is another department that has not been called. I may be running close to the end of my time, Mr. Chairman, but there is one point I should like to make. The hon. member for York-Sunbury is going to speak about this. I want to refer to the prisoners of war, and primarily those from Hong Kong. At this point I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) who, on June 22, put forward a resolution during private members hour dealing with these prisoners. I think we had a worth-while discussion amongst the few who had the opportunity to speak. I must say I did not appreciate the official attitude of the parliamentary secretary to the minister in this regard. I know we had a job to do and, personally, I do not believe he felt this way. However, this was the official attitude taken toward the discussion. Something definitely has to be done now, and we should not wait for these Hong Kong prisoners of war to come forward. The experiences of these men is quite different. Their numbers are small, approximately 1,200 now. There should be an independent survey made on the initiative of the Department of Veterans Affairs or under the aegis of the pension commission to ascertain how these men are faring 20 years later. We do know their mortality rate has been much higher.
I am not talking about the statistics we must get to prove that a man is suffering from a pensionable disability. I feel it is absolutely essential that, from the pension point of view, from the point of view of administration and pension predictability in the event the same situation should recur, we should ascertain what the negative effects

What has been the diminution in their capacity? Are they holding down second rate jobs or giving second rate performances as a result of this experience? I am not going to suggest this for myself, but some of my colleagues might: Are the prisoners of war from Europe giving a second rate performance? Immediately everybody might say, aye. Seriously, I should like to ask about the incidence of tuberculosis. Are these men going to be prematurely aged? Are we going to get more of these men needing domiciliary care under the war veterans allowance? The time to look into these cases is not when a man totters up to the pension commission and says, "Look, I am beat; will you look after me"? It is now, when you can give it more time. Look at him in his everyday surroundings, at how he is feeling, and see if his family life has been affected by these experiences. Has he been phychologically affected?
We have something to do here. This is one of the remaining tasks; and one can go further and say, let us look at the prisoners of war in Europe. I know some chaps who were knocked down in December 1939 and were still behind the wire in April 1945. I have seen men go wire-happy, which was the term used.
Two minutes.

Apparently the hon. member for Carleton finds these remarks a little extensive. I do not know what interest he may have in veterans but I do feel we should be doing something in this field, and anything we can get done in support of the proposal by the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) would be a step forward.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to prolong this debate by unnecessary repetition but I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West. I noticed that the parliamentary secretary was taking notes and I think he is very eager to reply. We look forward to listening to his response to the plea made by the hon.

member for Edmonton West with respect to the question of policy in connection with veterans hospitals, the study with respect to Hong Kong veterans, and the consideration of the conditions and circumstances of those who were prisoners of war in Europe.
I know that the hon. member for Edmonton West in dealing with this question was dealing with a subject that is treated on a strictly non-partisan basis. I am sure there are veterans in all parts of the chamber who are equally concerned about government policy with respect to veterans hospitals, but unlike the hon. member for Edmonton West I do not take a hidebound attitude. I realize we are living under changing conditions and circumstances and that in the public interest there will be some changes and improvements. But like the hon. member for Edmonton West, I would like to make certain none of those changes or, shall I say, improvements with respect to administration and the use of buildings affect the rights of veterans to receive the treatment and care they are guaranteed by the veterans charter.
I do hope that consideration is given to the plea made by the hon. member for Edmonton West, and previously by other hon. members, with respect to the study concerning the Hong Kong veterans, and the same applies to prisoners of war in Europe. These questions are all related and I know the parliamentary secretary is very interested in these problems. Another matter in which the Hong Kong veterans are particularly interested is getting a complete report on the disposition of the funds that were to be used for the alleviation of the circumstances of prisoners of war who suffered unusual hardship. With those brief remarks, and looking forward to hearing a reply on the part of the parliamentary secretary, I resume my seat.

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful to the hon. member for Edmonton West for raising the matters of veterans. As he has pointed out, there have been no meetings of the veterans affairs committee so far this session, and so this does provide the opportunity to bring up one or two matters of urgent interest. It is not my intention to discuss the business of the house. That has been ably done by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and others. Dealing with veterans affairs I would like to discuss a special group who are very dear to my heart, namely the Hong Kong veterans.
It is said that when a member of parliament is elected he should first work in the national interest, and second he should work

for the interests of his constituents; but I am sure that every hon. member, in addition to performing those two tasks, has certain groups in whom he is deeply interested. In my particular case for the last 20 years I have been deeply interested in the welfare of the veterans of our nation, veterans of the two world wars, of the Korean conflict, and those few who are left of the Boer war.
The matter of the Hong Kong veterans is a pressing one. It is a specially touching one because I think, of all the men who served in world war II those who were taken prisoners by the Japanese suffered more than any others. Perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton West, who was a gallant officer and was taken prisoner at Dieppe, or the hon. member for Yorkton who was also a prisoner, or the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, or the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, who did not suffer under the Japanese but under the Germans, would disagree. Because I come from a part of Canada that provided one of the regiments that served in Hong Kong, the Royal Rifles-the other was the Winnipeg Grenadiers-and because many of my kin served in Hong Kong and many did not return, due to brutality, torture and starvation, I am deeply interested in this group.
Over the past six or eight months I and a few others have been talking to those men who were prisoners of war at Hong Kong. They have submitted many facts to us in writing, and of course we ourselves know many of the facts. We know there were roughly 1,900 men there. We know that 300 were killed in the fighting of December 1941. But I think many people are too prone to forget that there were more than 300 Canadians who died of starvation, brutality and rough treatment in prison camps. It is on their behalf I speak now for a few minutes in this debate, and I make no apology for bringing their case forward at this time.
What have these ex-prisoners of war said? I would like to quote some of the things they have written to me, and I may say that all of these facts can be substantiated. They have said:
All Hong Kong veterans at the time of return from imprisonment showed the adverse effects of their experiences in varying degrees. The treatment which was provided then and subsequently has in many instances been beneficial but in many cases disability, either physical or psychological, remained. With the passage of time, the condition of many of these veterans has in fact deteriorated and it is the contention.. .that compensation in the nature of disability pensions has not shown an appropriate corresponding increase. In addition, that treatment for disability at D.V.A. treatment
Interim Supply
centres across Canada varies and should be brought to a uniform level.
The brief from which I am reading goes on to say that the diseases which occurred when they were prisoners of war and the complaints they have had since would seem to be of a permanent nature.
The reports which have appeared in medical literature show that the effects resulting from malnutrition and other diseases suffered by these veterans while P.O.W.'s are widespread and involve all body systems (central nervous system, cardiovascular system, genito-urinary system, gastrointestinal system etc.). It is the contention of the association that many diseases which have subsequently arisen among these veterans may well be related to the service-incurred disability. Particularly with reference to coronary disease, the association feels that the high incidence of this disease among Hong Kong veterans strongly suggests that there is a relationship with service-incurred disability and that evidence to the contrary is lacking.
The psychological stresses to which Hong Kong veterans were subjected during their period of imprisonment were severe and long continued. Four years of rough treatment, beatings and constant threat of torture in many forms, stress of undernourishment, inadequate clothing along with forced labour under intolerable conditions have left hidden personality scars which continue to lower these veterans' ability to adjust into normal civilian life.
I suppose other members have talked to those who have come back. There is the case of a young lad whom I knew very well; I taught him in school during my teaching career. This young lad was beaten to death by the Japanese with rifle butts because he did not obey an order. A year or so ago there was a series of programs on the C.B.C. radio, one of which dealt with the case of a prominent lady from Toronto who was in Singapore at the fall of that city and was taken prisoner. With her indomitable spirit she not only kept up the spirits of the other prisoners but perhaps kept alive many of those who were in prison camp with her. When she was released she was down to half her normal weight; she was covered with sores and scars. One of the things to which she had been subjected, according to her statement made on the radio, was the taking out of her teeth by the Japanese, without anaesthetic and with just a chisel and hammer. This is the kind of treatment to which these people were subjected. I suppose every one of us who has spoken to these men and women who were prisoners of war of the Japanese would have similar factual stories to relate.
I think in all the history of mankind the blackest chapter in the history of our civilization occurred in the ten years between 1935 and 1945 in Hitler's Germany, with

Interim Supply
the treatment of European Jewry. There is nothing to compare with that particularly black chapter in the history of mankind, when those people were stripped of all dignity and tortured and beaten to death. The same sort of thing happened to these men and a few women-not too many women-who were taken prisoner in Hong Kong; and, of course, to many, many women and thousands of male civilians and soldiers who were taken prisoner at Singapore and elsewhere in the Far East.
On behalf of this particular group I plead with the Minister of Veterans Affairs-I am sorry he is not here today; I am sure he is away on official business, but his parliamentary secretary is here-and I hope before this year is out this group of Hong Kong veterans will be listened to with sympathy, compassion and understanding, as I have said, of all those who served in our armed forces in world war II none suffered as did these particular men. I will continue reading what they have written to me:
As a result of this experience, many Hong Kong veterans show psychological disorders. Where a psychological disorder was evident immediately after return to Canada, the pension commission has recognized its relation to service. However, many Hong Kong veterans made a determined effort to readjust to a normal way of life and only after a passage of several years has it become evident that they are unable to do so. Therefore, the association contends that in all cases of psychological or emotional disturbances among Hong Kong veterans any question of doubt as to the relationship with service-connected disability should be resolved in favour of the veteran.
I see that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs is listening and I am sure he will agree with this. These veterans have made a series of suggestions to the veterans affairs committee of this house, and I have no doubt these suggestions were also made to previous veterans affairs committees. I would like to put them on the record again. They feel there should be a complete and thorough review of pensions in the case of Hong Kong veterans. Second, they ask for a revival of the survey that was started in 1950, and a yearly regular check-up of every individual who was a prisoner of war of the Japanese. They say there should be a thorough study of the effects of beri-beri, pelagra, dysentery, etc., to establish without question the connection with present disabilities such as optic atrophy, cardiac deficiencies, nerve destruction, stomach conditions, etc.
The Hong Kong veterans feel there should be an award of a minimum 50 per cent of pension for the residual effects of avitaminosis

in the case of every ex-Japanese prisoner of war of world war II. This is a contention with which I agree completely. Avitaminosis is of course a disease which is simply caused by malnutrition. These men have told me that they had as much rice as they could get in the palm of their hand, and that was all the food they had each day-they worked under slave labour conditions. The net result was that in many cases the weight of these men was reduced to only half their normal weight. I saw many of them before they left, because our embarkation leaves happened to coincide. When they went to Hong Kong in the fall of 1941 they were normal, healthy men, but they came back trembling, diseased and unable to continue in the professions and jobs they had before they enlisted.
They feel there should be an annual increase of 5 per cent of pension as from 1962 for the residual effects of avitaminosis caused by starvation. They ask that all ex-Hong Kong prisoners of war be given complete entitlement, and finally they ask that the Canadian pension commission review all cases where a Hong Kong veteran's death has been attributed to coronary thrombosis, especially where there is a history of beri-beri. The members of this group are much concerned about the many decisions in these cases to the effect that death was not attributable to service-related disabilities or conditions.
Mr. Chairman, I have made my plea on behalf of this very special group of Canadians who served their country in time of war and who I believe suffered more than any other Canadians in the defence of freedom. There are a number of other subjects I would like to cover. The hon. member for Edmonton West discussed the matter of veterans hospitals. I now understand that the negotiations in regard to the Colonel Belcher hospital and other veterans hospitals have ceased. I was told some time ago by the minister that with regard to the Lancaster military hospital, in which I have a special interest, there have been no discussions about its possible transfer to civilian control. However, I have no doubt that other members of the house will want to discuss that question.
There are many subjects which we could discuss in connection with veterans. I would like to pay my special tribute to the members of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I think this is an excellent department. I am not one of those who see horns on the heads of the members of the pension commission. I think they have done their job conscientiously. I feel very strongly about the war

veterans allowance board; I think that is one of the finest groups of men in the public service of this nation. The army benevolent fund has been exceptionally well administered over the years, as has the commonwealth war graves commission. I have had some experience with this body. 1 see the parliamentary secretary nodding agreement. No doubt he would concur in these particular sentiments. I would ask him to tell us, if he is going to speak later on behalf of his minister, what success he has had with the government in connection with the Newfoundland foresters. I remember that over the years he pleaded their case very strongly with the previous administration and I would be interested in knowing what success he is having on their behalf. Perhaps he would answer these questions a little later in this debate or when the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs are brought down. I will now yield the floor, Mr. Chairman, to others who wish to make their contribution in a most important debate for this most important group of Canadian citizens.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the time of this committee for a few moments. It is not often that 1 do this, but I have certain matters I wish to raise, particularly in regard to the Department of Veterans Affairs. However I should first like to refer to something which is much broader and probably of much more concern to the Canadian people. We are considering an interim supply bill in the amount of over $700 million. I submit the Canadian people are not aware of what is taking place in this house at the present time. A good deal of criticism has been made of this house by the people of the country, emanating I suppose from what they read, see and hear. I should like to ask this question of the government through you, Mr. Chairman. Why are we spending the time of the house talking about an interim supply bill of over $700 million when there are other more important matters which could be brought before us?
As I said earlier, it is very seldom I take the time of this committee or this house, but when we are asked to pass a bill involving over $700 million, without being given any details about it, it is time that some of us did take the time of this house to ask for that detail.
We have been asking questions but so far not too many answers have been given. We occasionally get an answer to the effect that everything is wonderful, business is good, employment is up. But what are the real facts?

There is more money
available for her today.

But it does not go as far as it did, when the cost of living index rises so rapidly. This is a very serious matter for most Canadians, particularly those who have a family to support. I am proud to admit that I am a father of six and a grandfather of four, so I know that when the cost of living index rises one point, or even a tenth of one point, it means something to the average Canadian. It does not apparently mean much across the way, but to those of us with certain limitations and only so much to spend it means a great deal.
Do not forget your garages.

I do not even have one garage. It is obvious you have a two-car garage.
We have been criticized for holding up legislation and that sort of thing. There is even talk that we are holding up the flag issue. This is not quite the case. The real issue, when we get down to it, is that we are asked to pass over $700 million worth of

Interim Supply
expenditures. That may not mean much to the Liberals, but to the average Canadian it means a lot. I can recall the time when they asked "What's a million"; but what is the answer to "what's $700 million"? That is the answer we want.
Where are the estimates? How long have we been here, looking for details of the estimates so that we can get down to the real facts? We have been told many times that business is much better, that employment is much better. How about the person who is not working? And how about the person who is working? Where does his money go and how much is it worth?
You are repeating yourself.

They are the questions we would like to ask.
I should like to deal with a particular department, the Department of Veterans Affairs. I appreciate the fact that is is a very important department, and I want to relate a branch of that department, the administration of the Veterans Land Act, to my own constituency. Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote from a letter which relates to what I said earlier. This letter is from a constituent complaining about a case which I investigated personally, during a special trip I made recently.
This gentleman has the following to say:
I am writing in complaint against V.L.A. in their recent decision to deny me a choice piece of acreage, for which I applied under the small holdings section of V.L.A.
I applied for a 20 acre farm one half mile south of Coaldale, on the main road, and could have bought it for the exceptionally low price of $8,000. It had clear title, power, good cistern, good outbuildings, including garage, machine shed, chicken-house, coal shed, granary, and cattle barn, also root cellar and two dugouts. The house was small, for our requirements, as I have five children, but there were three bedrooms, and at our own expense we were going to add to it, including running water, bathroom, in other words, completely modernize it. This could have all been done quite easily according to the local V.L.A. representative, and with least possible expense, as the house was ideally suited for this renovation. Again-I say-at our own expense.
The land was laid out perfectly for the project I had in mind, the raising of beef cattle. It was good land, easily irrigated and cross fenced exactly to suit my purpose.
The most important point is that It met my requirements for my family. It was five minutes from school, hospital and doctor, being as previously stated, only one half mile from Coaldale. The school bus stopped at the door, with my children being the last on in the morning, and the first off at night.
Ten years ago, V.L.A. paid $7,300 for the 20 acres adjacent to this property and it had abso-

lutely nothing on it except a house not comparable to the one on the site I wanted. There was no power, fences, outbuildings, and the only road to it was a quarter mile dirt road through a beet field.
V.L.A. could have purchased this property for me at exactly the same price (the power making up the $700 difference) as this they bought ten years ago, and there is no comparison between the two, the one I wanted being far superior in all respects. The value of the land alone has more than doubled the past ten years in this area.
The most frustrating part of all is that it was passed by the local office, with a strong recommendation, passed by Calgary district office, and then turned down by Edmonton office. This I cannot begin to comprehend.. .what is the economics of paying local V.L.A. representatives $7,000 per annum, men in Calgary in the district office more, only to have their recommendations totally ignored by someone in Edmonton (who must be in an even higher salary bracket) who apparently knows nothing of conditions in our own locale? What are these men hired for?
On Edmonton's letter of refusal, they stated that I should acquire suitable property and then build a house on it under V.L.A. It appears quite apparent that V.L.A. does not want to establish veterans on small holdings, but rather have them build minimum $12,000 homes under their V.L.A. grant. Is this true? If so, the small holdings portion of the V.L.A. should be immediately repealed, before other veterans and their families are led down the garden path-only to be disappointed, frustrated and made sick at heart-as was mine. If this is not true

and the government is sincere in providing for a veteran under this portion of the act-then someone in a position of some authority is making a mockery of it, and should be made answer for it-
I have not read the entire letter, Mr. Chairman. I should like to point out a suggestion in answer to this man's request as stated in the second paragraph of a letter dated March 6, 1964, by a district supervisor. He has stated:
It is suggested that you endeavour to locate an acreage without improvements and apply to this administration for a loan to build a home more in keeping with the needs of your family.
A director followed the practice laid down by this department and stated the property was inadequate and unsuitable, mainly because of the dwelling, a small four-room frame building lacking the accepted conveniences, with the exception of electricity. We find that two different officials of the same department have come to entirely different conclusions.
I am sorry the minister is not present at this time because I feel sure he could explain this situation. At one point the individual concerned is told to find property without any building at all, and on another occasion told to find property with a more adequate house.
I understand there is a further policy to the effect that the price for a property should

relate to the price of adjacent property. The property involved in this case was offered for approximately half the price received for an adjacent property.
Mr. Chairman, in view of the attitude expressed in this letter and the attitudes expressed by members here you can understand why we desire to examine the estimates of the various departments. I am sure the members on this side of the chamber are willing to come to some agreement, even one in respect of the flag debate, in order that we may thoroughly examine the estimates.
May I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Chairman, when I was dealing with interim supply before the recess I pointed out to the committee that there were certain points that members of the official opposition wanted to discuss, and we hoped we would be able to do so before dealing with other legislation. I mentioned to the committee the fact that when we are considering over $700 million in supply it should be our prerogative to discuss the matters in detail. I wanted to bring this to the attention of the committee, and even at the expense of repeating myself I do so again for the sole purpose of emphasizing that when we are asked to consider the granting of an amount of $700 million in a very short time it is hardly fair that the official opposition should be criticized for filibustering or obstructing, or whatever word may be used in this connection. To the Canadian people and certainly to myself as the representative of a particular area of this country an amount of $700 million is not something to be considered lightly.
I have asked why we have not been given the opportunity to deal with the estimates in detail. After all, we have been here for many months, and no one knows better than you, Mr. Chairman, that we have been here for so long and have yet to consider in detail estimates which amount to much more than $700 million in total.
I referred earlier to some of the answers we get. Earlier today we heard a respected member of the government relate the many good things that have happened under the present government. The gross national product is up, employment is up. But I should
Interim Supply
like to remind the government and other hon. members opposite that there are other things that should be considered in detail, and the main one is the estimates.
There is something the Canadian people should realize with reference to the cost of living index. How rapidly has the cost of living index increased in relation to the increase in the gross national product, the decrease in unemployement and so on? Is it not a relative thing? I said earlier and I repeat by way of emphasis that when housewives across Canada, particularly the wives of veterans, spend a dollar, what do they have for it when they get home?
I referred earlier to the complaint of a particular veteran with relation to the Veterans Land Act. I quoted a certain letter and certain reactions of the department and I took some exception to the answers given. Admittedly I was trying to relate the matter to certain actions or lack of action or reaction on the part of the government. Maybe someone is at fault and maybe not, but what is involved is a matter of service to a particular Canadian citizen who is a bona fide veteran and who made a bona fide request to the Department of Veterans Affairs and received a certain answer. Probably this involves a grievance and it may not even be in order, but I have brought this matter to the attention of the government and have raised one or two points in connection with it by way of a specific instance of something that should be considered by the minister when we are dealing with interim supply.
By way of summary, though it may be more than that, there is a rumour in my constituency-it is related to the grievance I raised earlier-that the V.L.A. office is going to be closed or curtailed. I would offer my prayers that this will not happen. I have referred to the service that is provided in our area. I could go into a great deal of detail about the number of veterans located in the area covered by this office whose territory extends to the Saskatchewan border and practically to Calgary. There is some thought of closing the office or curtailing the service in this area. This may be a grievance but my main point is that this office should not be closed or curtailed. Actually the service of the office should be improved. If that were done it is probable that complaints of this kind would not have to be brought to the attention of the house. But here is a case of a bona fide Canadian citizen and veteran who is concerned about his right to benefit from

Interim, Supply
the veterans affairs legislation, particularly the Veterans Land Act. I have referred to this matter in some detail, though not completely because I wanted to save the time of the house.
I appreciate very much, Mr. Chairman, the time that I have been allotted. I reiterate however that I have taken very little of the time of this house or of these committees. If this sort of thing continues, then I and many others on this side of the house will take much more time, as I believe we should. Perhaps I may refer to certain writings of a gentleman by the name of Brown who, very early and before the articles of confederation were finalized, drew attention of people interested to the fact that a member speaking in the House of Commons was not limited to a 30-minute speech or a 40-minute speech. He sometimes continued speaking until four or five o'clock in the morning and then resumed at two o'clock in the afternoon, for a good purpose. I believe this gentleman named Brown may have been defined as a Liberal reformer at one time, and he pointed out that these facts should not be buried.
As I said earlier, some of these facts have been buried right here in this motion for interim supply. I want to ask where we find the time to discuss interim supply? I am not obstructing, I am not filibustering. I am asking a simple question, Mr. Chairman. Where is the time to discuss these very important issues?

Since this is the time to ask questions, I should like to ask a few questions concerning veterans affairs. I note that the veterans affairs committee, which is a standing committee of the House of Commons, last met on December 10, 1963. I cannot understand, and I should like to ask the minister, why the estimates of veterans affairs could not have been sent to that committee. We would have had an opportunity to go through them, and perhaps everything that was said in the committee would have been repeated in the house; but at least we would have had competent witnesses before the committee and we would have been able to get answers to a few of our questions.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister and the government to the fact that the veterans affairs committee reported to the house on December 10, 1963. This report contained certain recommendations. I assume that the chairman of the committee, being a member of the government, is in close liaison with his minister. Since December we have

not heard one thing about veterans affairs, except the taking over of veterans hospitals. I should like to ask if this department has given any consideration to section 70 of the Pension Act, the benefit of the doubt clause. I should like to refer the members of the committee to paragraph 8 of the report of the veterans affairs committee. We have not heard anything from the Department of Veterans Affairs since the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek brought a private bill before us touching on this very problem. It was adopted in the house and referred to the committee. All the witnesses and the committee agreed that some small amendment should be made to insure that the original spirit of the act was being carried out.
In other words, it was decided that the veteran was not on trial before the commission. The commission should give him the benefit of the doubt and if there were any questions, the benefit of the doubt would go to the veteran. I should like to know if the government intends to do anything about this. I think it is important to a good many thousands of men.
Another thing to which I should like to refer is the appeal board. May I read one of the recommendations presented by this committee, after a great deal of impartial study and the hearing of impartial witnesses. Paragraph 10 of the report reads:
Your committee further feels that instead of a "one-shot" appeal which is both final and binding, there should be two appeals as follows:
(a)	a preliminary appeal in which all the evidence is transcribed and then a ruling is given in the form of a written judgment in which all points of evidence, both medical and legal on which the ruling is based is set forth in writing and signed.
(b)	a second ruling as at present. Your committee recommends that this procedure would correct the disadvantage the veteran now suffers as he would know what arguments must be rebutted instead of having to prepare his appeal blindly as at present.
Now, according to the evidence given by both the veterans organizations and the department, a veteran is not supplied with the proper information on which to base an appeal. I think it is only fair that this should be done and there should be a regulation or a directive from the department to this effect. Where does the veteran go to secure this information? I feel that a mimeographed sheet should be sent to a veteran setting forth the various steps in the appeal procedure.
The veterans rights are being looked after better than ever before. We have more people interested, and we have our service organ-

izations. However, there are still some veterans who are left out on a limb. These things are not being done. They have been recommended. If the government feels there is no reason for them to be done, then let the government tell us. I feel that the procedure is a trifle arbitrary when you consider that most of these men are kept in the dark. I know you cannot help it, but you can help them find their way.
Well, those are two points mentioned in this report which have never been brought before this house by the government, which has responsibility for introducing legislation. There is one more thing I should like to mention, namely the Hong Kong veterans. This subject was mentioned in the committee, and of course we know the Hong Kong veteran is in a special position, for a special reason. Not only was he in the cage for four years but he suffered malnutrition. He suffered both mental and physical abuse and was almost without hope. Officials of the department may say, "Oh, well, 1,200 of them are getting pensions;" but we ask for a breakdown of those pensions and of the reasons why they are given.
What studies are being made with regard to Asiatic prisoners of war, and when I say Asiatic prisoners of war I mean studies by Great Britain, Australia and the United States, which countries have undertaken special studies. Our last study, I believe, was in 1950, and I feel it is time a little positive action was taken by the Department of Veterans Affairs, which may be beginning to feel that its activities and usefulness are over. They are not over and will not be over until the last veteran dies.
I believe that the intent which parliament had when it passed this legislation is not being carried out. I would not like to say where the fault lies but I believe there should be a reorganization of the department. I appreciate that this is a very difficult problem for any government, but I believe minor changes in the legislation could also assist.
The hon. member who preceded me spoke about V.L.A. and small holdings loans. Everyone knows that in case after case the judgments handed down are not consistent. If we must have regulations let them apply to the whole country and provide for the right of appeal. Too often veterans have been turned down when they wished to acquire a piece of land worth $7,500 and later that same piece of land has been bought by civilians for $15,000. There should be an appeal from these rulings, and again I ask why the
Interim Supply
committee on veterans affairs cannot at least have a look at the estimates of the department?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few brief minutes to reply to the questions that have been raised, particularly with respect to veterans hospitals and treatment services for the Hong Kong veterans. In order to allay any fears that might exist in the minds of hon. members, and even in the minds of veterans, with respect to veterans hospitals I should like to repeat the assurance given by the Prime Minister at the 20th dominion convention of the Royal Canadian Legion, at Winnipeg on May 17 last. Speaking to that convention the Prime Minister said, and I quote from page 43 of The Legionary, July 1964 issue:
Tonight I want to say merely this. All those who have examined the problem know that it is changing and that, in the interests of the veterans, changes may have to be made in dealing with it.
The government has no intention, however, of trying to solve these new problems overnight, or of adopting either a cavalier or a casual attitude towards the matter. Certain fears have been expressed in this regard by the Legion and by veterans which I am sure will not materialize.
I can assure you tonight that in anything we seek to do about veterans medical and hospital care the government's primary consideration will be to protect the interests and promote the welfare of the veterans themselves. They are not problems but people. Veterans, especially older veterans, deserve and must receive special and humane and generous consideration. There will be no change which will remove control of veterans' admissions and their treatment and their domiciliary care from the Department of Veterans Affairs. That department is not going out of business. Its responsibilities are not going to be reduced. Moreover, there will be full consultation by the department with veterans' organizations in the area before any changes are made.
We have only one concern: to guarantee to our veterans the high standard of treatment and service to which they are entitled and must continue to be entitled-even in the face of the doctor shortage and the changing nature of the patient load in our D.V.A. hospitals.
I repeat: we are not following a rigid course or one which is intended in a short time to solve all hospital and related problems. We are not going to rush into any radical change, and we are not going to make any change of any kind that will operate against the interests and the welfare of the veterans.
It is our duty to continue to ensure the highest standards of medical treatment available. It is, of course, our duty also to effect economies where possible but only when compatible with the standards I have mentioned, and never at the expense of the needs and the interests of veterans whose care indeed may require more, rather than less, expenditure by government. Their welfare comes first.
With respect to negotiations for hospitals the department has not taken any initiative

Interim Supply
and never intended to take any initiative in this matter. The situation was that the department was interested in inviting proposals on certain terms, and these terms were very clearly specified at the same dominion convention in Winnipeg on May 18, by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. For the information of the committee I would again quote from The Legionary at page 47, where the minister said:
Now, let me summarize the situation:
1.	The objective is to ensure the highest possible standard of care;
2.	We must have absolute, guaranteed priority for active treatment in any hospital where operational control may be transferred to another authority;
3.	Veterans will report to D.V.A. medical staff on the premises, and D.V.A. staff will continue to have full authority to decide when a veteran is to be admitted to hospital or discharged. They will also decide who will occupy the priority beds we will have;
4.	Domiciliary care institutions, satisfactory to D.V.A. medical staff, must be available, and priority use guaranteed;
5.	And of course we must ensure adequate safeguards for our staff where any changes in operational control may become effective.
These are very stringent terms and not many agencies are in a position to meet them.
Dealing with individual hospitals referred to by the hon. member for Edmonton West, negotiations with regard to Colonel Belcher hospital in Calgary were discontinued and this was caused mainly by delay in drawing up agreements containing suitable guarantees to safeguard the interests of the veterans. With respect to the Edmonton domiciliary home negotiations are still going on. Government house was offered to the Alberta government in exchange for a modem nursing building which would be operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs. We have to be satisfied that this building will meet all our requirements. With regard to the Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital, nobody has shown any interest or put forward any proposals. The same thing is true of Lancaster hospital, in which the hon. member for York-Sunbury is interested. However, with respect to Ridgewood hospital, negotiations are going on with the workmen's compensation board, who will continue to use this hospital for rehabilitation purposes and arrange for the same number of beds to be available for veterans as are in use at the present time. At Sunnybrook in Toronto we have rented an empty ward at cost to Wellesley hospital, and in it they have set up an arthritic unit which is working extremely well. So much for the individual hospitals.

I should now like to spend a few minutes dealing with the question of Hong Kong veterans. Reference was made to a motion by the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) which was talked out. I remember that occasion very well because I had that very unpleasant duty myself. I can assure the committee that I was not very happy in discharging it, but I felt it was in the interests of veterans to do so. With regard to surveys on Hong Kong veterans, there have been several surveys in past years. The first survey was carried out in 1950 by Dr. Crawford who is now the director general of medical services. He was in service at that time and was borrowed by the department to make this particular survey, and his report was published. Five years afterwards another survey was carried out by Dr. J. D. Adamson, who found that 30 per cent of the Hong Kong veterans had quite serious disability which had a sound pathological base, another 30 per cent had a variety of complaints which could not be attributed to discernible pathological causes, and a further 30 per cent were found to be in very good condition. In addition to that, special surveys have been carried out-one with regard to visual defects-in Quebec city and in Toronto. A survey with respect to psychoneurosis has been going on for just about a year. The standing committee on veterans affairs recommended a survey, in their report last December. It is to be found at page 430 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 13, and is recommendation No. 14:
In view of the special problems that time and experience have revealed concerning the Hong Kong veterans this committee urges that a special study and survey be made of their problems and particularly disabilities.
The Canadian pension commission acted immediately on this recommendation of the standing committee on veterans affairs and began to take steps to set a survey in motion. It takes several months to plan such a survey and to negotiate all the arrangements that have to be made regarding personnel and the facilities to carry it out. When the motion sponsored by the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) came before the house this survey was just getting under way. There are very few Hong Kong veterans; the sample is hardly big enough to carry out even one survey. One survey, as I said, has been going on for nearly a year and a second survey has been initiated by the Canadian pension commission. To superimpose a third survey on top of that would be totally impracticable. We were then faced with the problem of discon-

tinuing this one and placing responsibility elsewhere, or vetoing the motion of the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.). It does not seem right that six months work should be wasted in this way, because this is preliminary work that would be essential in any case and would have to be done before any further study could be initiated by the standing committee.
With respect to pensions entitlement and pension assessments, hon. members know that these are medical decisions. The pension commission, under the present legislation and until that legislation is changed, have sole responsibility for interpreting the pension act and administering it, and nothing we can do can alter that fact, unless we change the legislation. In any case, Mr. Chairman, most of these decisions are based on medical judgments and as lay people we have to accept the best medical advice we can get.

Mr. Chairman, first of all may I thank the hon. member for Yorkton for his reference to the bill I introduced in this house, Bill No. C-7. I intend, if my time does not run out, to make further reference to that bill. While I am in this grateful mood I would also like to say thank you to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. At least we are now getting answers, and if all along we had been given answers such as the parliamentary secretary has given this evening, we would not have had to debate that matter in the house this afternoon. Answers are what the opposition have been after. While I am on the subject of the parliamentary secretary, I will say-and I think I speak for all members of the standing committee on veterans affairs-that we only regret that when the cabinet was formed by the present administration, the hon. member was not made minister of veterans affairs.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Yorkton, myself and many others in this house have been members of that standing committee ever since we were elected to parliament, and we know the parliamentary secretary has been a very ardent worker in it and a very reasonable member to deal with. I am quite sure that if he had been made minister of veterans affairs the problems we are speaking about tonight would not have arisen, particularly in regard to veterans hospitals. I intended to say something on that subject, but in view of his explanation I will refrain from doing so.
I have mentioned Bill No. C-7 that I introduced into the house. I introduced another
Interim Supply
bill this session, with regard to war veterans allowances. Because of the introduction of those two bills I have received from all across Canada, and not just from my own constituency, a great deal of correspondence from veterans who have complaints. The most recent correspondence I have received in this connection has been in regard to the increase in the cost of living. This may not be important as far as the government is concerned, but with the increased cost of living is coupled another problem, that of inflation. I think the government should go along with us by bringing down the estimates, when we could look into these two problems.
I know some members of the committee tonight will say, "What about the increased cost of living? It is a buoyant economy; nobody is suffering because of the increased cost of living". However, I would suggest to those who say this that if they had received some of the letters I have received from these pensioners who are on a fixed, low income, they would appreciate that it does mean something to them. I am not blaming the government for the increase in the cost of living, but I would suggest to the government that this is one of the things they should be watching, and inflation is another. One of the things the economists tell us is that the way to inflation is excessive government expenditures, a matter we have been trying to discuss for 118 days. But the government has only let us deal so far with two departments.
The government should be concerned about the expenditures which have been taking place. Perhaps there are answers for this; we do not know. The committee heard this afternoon about the number of questions which have been asked and the very few answers received in reply. Perhaps our system of parliament has outlived itself like the parliament of France, although I am not prepared to debate that. However, I suggest that if any hon. members watched television last night and saw the hon. member for York East and the hon. member for Essex South, it would have been a revelation to them. It conveyed to me the impression that we in the opposition were not the only people concerned about what was going on in this house. I commend them for that program and I suggest it is regrettable that all hon. members did not see this program and listen to the very constructive suggestions which were made. These two hon. members referred to what we have asked for ever since the session started, and that is for more work to be

Interim Supply
given to standing committees. Estimates should be referred to our standing committees. As they said last night, the backbenchers on the government side feel they are not doing the job they were sent here to do. We on this side of the house also feel that the government is not allowing us to do the job we are supposed to do.
I said the other day that our main purpose as members of the opposition is to examine the estimates of the government and to scrutinize its expenditures. For some reason the government has been concealing these from us, and that is our cry. Possibly this is one reason, if it is the case, that the people of Canada think that parliament is not doing anything. I am sure that everyone in the committee tonight will admit that we have done practically everything we can to force the government to bring down the estimates.
Prolong the debate.

That could be, but I would say this to the hon. member, that very seldom since he came to the house have I heard him get up and make a speech. It appears to me that his prime object in being here is to interject, and sometimes sarcastically. If that is why his constituents sent him to parliament I am sure Hansard should record this fact so that his constituency is aware of it.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

When I have finished. Two of the main components in the consumers price index which have contributed to the increased cost of living, I am told by economists, are the question of housing and the question of food. Why housing comes first I am not sure, and I am not particularly concerned with housing. Perhaps one of the reasons it is a factor is because of the 11 per cent tax which the government put on and which the opposition tried to get removed. But I am concerned about the cost of food because I represent an agricultural area. I am concerned at the price of grain and the price of cattle, they being the two main industries in my constituency. I am not going to say too much about grain at the moment but I do want to say a few words about the price of cattle.
In a question I asked a week or 10 days ago I made reference to the British market and I asked the government what steps it had taken to gain a portion of that market. There were two reasons I asked the question. One was because at one time we had a

portion of the British market while today we do not; the other was because of the fear of drought on the prairies. I see the Minister of Agriculture is leaving but I should like him to wait a few moments and to explain to the house why the producer on the prairies -this was also a matter raised by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale the other day-only receive in the neighbourhood of 16 cents a pound for his cattle while the consumer in the east apparently pays as much as $1.39 a pound. There is quite a gulf between those two figures. I admit that the 16 cents a pound to which I refer is live weight, and those who know anything about butchering say that this meat dresses out about 40 to 60 per cent. Therefore, if we make it an even 50 per cent, let us call it 32 cents a pound. Why is there this spread between what the producer on the prairies receives and what the consumer in the urban area pays?
The reason I ask this question is that in my remarks to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce I suggested that the top price in Canada for choice cuts was around 79 cents a pound. Then two days after I put that question I received a letter from a lady in Montreal asking me where she could get choice cuts or any kind of cuts for 79 cents a pound. In fact she enclosed with her letter a number of purchase slips which she had obtained from a departmental store in Montreal which show that a T-bone steak costs $1.39 a pound, sirloin steak $1.29 a pound, cube steak $1.25 a pound, flank steak 95 cents a pound and ground round steak 89 cents a pound. I suggested that the top price in Canada was around 79 cents a pound so I was amazed when I saw that this was what the consumer was paying for meat in eastern Canada.
I am suggesting that the minister should go to the Department of Justice and ask the investigation branch of that department to look into this wide spread in price, I can see why people in eastern Canada do not understand what is happening in western Canada when they pay $1.39 for T-bone steaks, when the average received by the producers in western Canada is 32 cents a pound. It seems to me that something is wrong.
Perhaps I am in error but I suggest that it is the government's responsibility to look into these inequities. There may be an explanation. I know that the meat has to be handled several times before it gets on to the

counters of the retail stores; but it also seems to me that whoever handles it must be getting a great deal more profit than the producer is getting. That is where there is such a great misunderstanding between the people in the west and the people in the east.
I presume that the same applies in the case of grain or, if you like, bread. I would request the minister to look into this matter and give the people of Canada the explanation to which I think they are entitled. I think it is the duty of the government to investigate such matters as this. I am not blaming them, but I would ask the government what they have done about matters like this. I suggest that this is more the business of the government than the red herring they have drawn across the floor of this house in the name of the flag. I believe that is not parliament's responsibility.
I should like to say a few words about inflation. Economists state that there are six major problems resulting from inflation, and I suggest they are evident ones. It is the responsibility of the government to let the people of Canada know whether there is a danger of inflation and to reassure them if there is not. I am very pleased that there is a buoyant economy in Canada, although I am not so pleased that the Liberal government is in power. I think the reason for that buoyant economy stems from the measures put into effect by the Conservative government when they were in power. I suggest devaluation was one way of accomplishing this. There are many other suggestions I should like to make, but I am pleased there is a buoyant economy in Canada. I suggest the government should be investigating these signs of inflation and reassuring the people of Canada that inflation is not going to take place.
I should now like to refer to six problems which economists tell us we are facing. First, they suggest inflation aggravates labour and management tensions. I have listened to debates and answers to questions in the House of Commons over at least the past week or ten days which indicate that labour-management problems are brewing and that they hit low income groups more severely than others. I have received letters from pensioners, and I am sure other members have received similar letters, which indicate that the recent increase in pensions passed by this parliament has been offset by the increase in the cost of living. I am surprised that this increase is no longer serving the purpose we thought it would serve when it was passed.
Interim Supply
The third result of inflation is a spurring in general social unrest. As far as I am aware there has been more social unrest in Canada in the last nine or ten months than I can remember at any time during the history of Canada, and I should like to remind hon. members that I am not as young as some of them.
Inflation also destroys public confidence in our currency, and destroys incentive to save. It dries up the capital and pushes up interest rates. The Minister of Finance is in the chamber and I hope he will tell the people there is no danger of an increase in interest rates. I should like to pose several other questions for him to answer when he does speak. I should like him to assure the people of Canada that when the next budget is presented the deficit will not be more than $1 billion. I would like to discuss this situation further at some later date, but intend at this time to say a few words in reply to the hon. member for Yorkton, and his reference to the recommendation of the standing committee on veterans affairs. My remarks will also have relation to the television program of last night to which I have referred.
The suggestion was made by one of the hon. members who participated in that program that we refer more of our estimates to different committees of the house, and the reasoning behind this suggestion is sound. One of the hon. members stated he had 20 years experience in municipal affairs, and pointed out that municipal and city councils established various committees to study estimates. These committees consider the estimates, obtaining answers to questions asked and report back with recommendations to the council. He pointed out further that very often following this consideration questions were asked by members who were not either on the committee or not satisfied with the answers obtained, but that a great deal of time was saved by this procedure.
The hon. members who participated in that program suggested that a similar procedure or practice should be followed by this parliament. I agree with the suggestion; but as the member for Yorkton said, last year a very thorough investigation took place during meetings of the committee on veterans affairs as a result of which recommendations were made to the House of Commons as well as to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I should like to refer to several of those recommendations.
I have before me the third report to the House of Commons of the standing committee on veterans affairs. This report indicates that

Interim Supply
the hon. member tor Kootenay West was concerned with Bill No. C-13. The committee recommended in respect oi that bill as follows:
With respect to the subject matter of Bill C-13. it was unanimously agreed that more effective steps should be taken to observe November 11 as a national holiday and a solemn day of remembrance in all parts of Canada.
As a result of that statement the committee recommended as follows:
In this connection your committee recommends that this matter be made the subject of federal-provincial discussions with a view to attaining the desired objective.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary, in the absence of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, what steps have been taken in respect of that recommendation of the standing committee which was composed of members from all parties.
The point I am attempting to make is that there is no purpose to be served by committees meeting and making recommendations unless the house or government acts upon them.
Some reference was made last night on the television program to that situation, and I do not think I am revealing anything I should not reveal in stating that one of the backbenchers on the government side made certain proposals to the treasury benches, which were received with little indication of acceptance.
Another recommendation made by the committee on veterans affairs reads as follows:
Your committee was Impressed with the amount of evidence that seemed to indicate that the original and obvious intention of parliament as set forth in section 70 of the Pension Act (benefit of doubt clause) is not uniformly applied in that case where the circumstances appear to be identical or extremely similar received quite different rulings.
This recommendation dealt with cases of cancer and multiple sclerosis which developed while veterans were in the armed services. Usually in cases of this kind the ruling of the pension commission is that the condition is not attributable to war services. I should like to know how in the name of heaven the pension commission can make that ruling in view of the fact the medical profession is not aware of the cause of cancer or multiple sclerosis.
The report of that committee then continues:
There was general agreement In committee that this situation should be corrected. There was unanimous support for the purpose of Bill C-7 and substantial support for the principle involved.

Hon. members will recall that Bill No. C-7 proposed to allow judicial appeal from rulings of the Canadian pension commission. Most members are aware that the Pension Act, as I refer to it, is one of the few acts passed by this parliament in respect of which the judiciary in our country cannot rule. Parliament through error or necessity when this bill was presented and passed in this house included section 5(5) which stated that the interpretation was the sole responsibility of the pension commission. Clause 70, which I believe is the benefit of doubt clause, was also included. I believe the explanation given in this regard by the member for Yorkton is correct.
I should like to have had time to read into the record the report of Lord Denning's maiden speech in the British House of Commons, in which he refers to exactly the same point I have made in respect of Bill C-7. Fortunately the committee made this recommendation to the government, and I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs what action the government has taken, and what direction has been given by the minister to the pension commission. If he suggests his hands are bound because of the act, I should like to know what action he will instigate to amend the act. I think possibly it is time the interpretation section of this act was amended, taking the responsibility for interpretation out of the hands of the commission and making it subject to judiciary ruling, as is the case in respect of all other acts passed by this parliament.
Recommendation No. 9 of that committee reads as follows:
Your committee feels that the time has come when major pieces of pensions legislation should be reviewed and is of the opinion that much of the difficulty can be overcome by reviewing the sections in question so as to clarify the following points:
(a)	'Benefit of doubt'. At the moment there is some evidence to show that the interpretation now being given by the commissioners is not sufficiently broad to be entirely in keeping with what we believe to be the spirit of the act.
I might also say that is true of the intention of parliament at the time it passed this act. The interpretation that the pension commission put on that cannot be disputed because they have the sole power to interpret the act in any manner they wish.
We suggest that the word "doubt" in the phrase "benefit of doubt" be interpreted to mean "a reasonable doubt" as might be expected to arise in the mind of a reasonable man in the street.
(b)	That the burden of proof rests with the commission and not with the veteran applicant.

I would say again: See the extract from Lord Denning's report. The tenth recommendation that the committee presented to the house was as follows:
Your committee further feels that instead of a "one shot" appeal which is both final and binding, there should be two appeals as follows:
(a)	a preliminary appeal in which all the evidence is transcribed and then ruling is given in the form of a written judgment in which all points of evidence, both medical and legal, on which the ruling is based is set forth in writing and signed.
(b)	a second ruling as at present. Your committee recommends that this procedure would correct the disadvantage the veteran now suffers as he would know what arguments must be rebutted instead of having to prepare his appeal blindly as at present.
I suggest to the hon. member for Essex South and the hon. member for York East that if their suggestion were implemented and these estimates and the proposal they have made were sent to the committee, another thing we would have to guard against would be inaction on the part of the members on the treasury benches in regard to the proposals made by the committee. I would suggest that maybe these two members at some future date or even now could get up in the house and explain their proposal, because I think it has merit and the house should consider it. But this is one problem that would have to be overcome.
The committee on veterans affairs is, I think, a non-partisan committee. Very seldom have I ever heard politics discussed or reference made that one member belonged to a different party from that of a member speaking. It was one of the best committees of the House of Commons to work on, and I cannot remember any time when its decisions were not unanimous with regard to proposals to the government.
But what good is a recommendation of this sort if the government will not act on it? I am inclined to think that possibly the time we spent in this committee was wasted because, as the hon. member for Yorkton said, the report was submitted last December and to date apparently no action has been taken. I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to get up and tell us what has happened to the report submitted to the government, and particularly to his minister. I would be pleased if he would explain what action, if any, has been taken.
