Mr. Chairman, the mood of the house today seems to be inclined toward the answering of questions that have been propounded during the course of the discussion. I think it will be recalled that on Friday last when I entered the debate in connection with the consideration of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration several questions were propounded to me. While I protested at the time that I was not the responsible minister, I feel that inasmuch as the questions from government backbenchers arose because of certain statements I had made I should at least have the courtesy to reply to two of them.
In the first place, the hon. member for Carleton questioned my statement concerning the immigration policy enunciated by the government of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King which, when it was analysed carefully, indicated that there was discrimination in terms of ethnic and cultural matters. I informed the hon. member for Carleton at that time that he would find the statement recorded in Hansard and I also intimated that I would look up the record for him and reply in the house. It is found in the record for Friday, February 18, 1955. The statement is included in a speech that was made by the then minister of citizenship and immigration, Hon. Walter Harris. I quote the statement:
Mr. King, then prime minister, said that immigration should not and would not alter the fundamental character of our people. Mr. King, I believe, meant two things by that phrase: (a) that the racial background of our people would be maintained within reasonable balance, and because he was not a Presbyterian for nothing, he also meant (b) that we would avoid an influx of persons whose viewpoint differed substantially from that of the average, respectable God-fearing Canadian.
That statement is recorded on page 1288 of Hansard for that date. He went on to say:
It is true that from time to time racial origin may not be in balance and some alarmists might be concerned about a temporary trend, but we should judge the results on the over-all period. For example, we have always felt that the British people should represent the greater proportion of our immigrants and we have done our best to increase the flow from the United Kingdom in the past four years, realizing that the figure of 13,000 at that time was too low. The figure has risen steadily to over 48,000 this past year.

Interim Supply
At the same time, one cannot disregard the advantages of having a mixed population and of adding to those other national groups already here who have demonstrated their ability to adapt themselves to Canadian conditions.
I think that will substantiate the observation I made on Friday last that it was high time that the government of Canada moved to broaden its immigration regulations so that they would be more in tune with the prevailing humanitarian spirit of the post-war world. This is precisely what was done in the year 1962, and as we examine the immigration records year by year since the new regulations began to be implemented I am sure we will see the broadening base for immigration to this country.
Arising from that statement the hon. member for Hamilton West posed another question to me in which he asked whether a certain order in council approved by the government in 1959 was not of a discriminatory nature, inasmuch as it restricted immigration from certain European countries-he did not specify which countries-to sponsored immigrants. I can only reply as I intended to reply last Friday afternoon, when unfortunately I was interrupted so frequently that my time expired and I did not have the opportunity. But I can only add to the explanation I gave on Friday afternoon last, that this was a problem right across the board with respect to our regulations previous to 1962. They restricted immigration to Canada to sponsored immigrants and those from the United Kingdom or western Europe. I do not see how this in any way detracts from the fundamental change that was made in the amendments to the regulations in 1962.
I had intended also to say a brief word at that time concerning what I regard as the next or perhaps the most important function of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I refer, of course, to the welfare of Canada's first citizens or to the group that should be regarded as the first citizens. Certainly they were here long before any other Canadians arrived. I refer to our Canadian Indian population. It has often been said that if the North American Indians had been more selective in their immigration policy there would be no problem for them at the present time.
I think it is quite fitting that one of the most effective presentations that was put before the first meeting of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism here in the city of Ottawa last year was made by Mrs. Ethel Brant Monture, who is a descendant of one of the great chiefs of the Six Na-

tions Indians. She pointed out that if there is any priority as far as racial or ethnic groups are concerned in this country, certainly her people have the No. 1 priority. She went further and pointed out that racism, as such, should have gone out with the horrors of world war II, which were perpetrated by the Nazi politicians whose whole philosophy of government was based on race and narrow nationalism. She made the point that the time had arrived to speak of Canadians as a whole and not speak in terms of Canadians derived from their ethnic or racial origins. It was not surprising that that presentation, coming from an outstanding spokesman of Canada's first citizens, received a resounding vote of confidence in the applause of the people who had gathered for that first session.
It is not necessary to review Canada's record in regard to the treatment of our Indian population. This has been done many times in the house. There was a time during the consideration of the estimates of the department of Indian affairs when hon. members gave scant attention. It is rather interesting to note that since the Indians received the vote there have been more speeches on behalf of them during the discussion of estimates, be they supplementary, interim or main estimates, than ever hitherto. I do not want to place myself in that category because I was interested in this problem long before the Indians received the vote, which I believe was in 1959.
My interest derived from the fact that I had two reservations in my constituency, both of which accommodated large groups of Sioux Indians who had settled in Canada after escaping from the United States following the Custer massacre. My contact with these two reservations has convinced me down through the years that there has been neglect; there has been discrimination; there has been segregation in the attitude of the government of Canada toward these first citizens. However, the record is improving, and I want to be positive in the few remarks I make tonight. There has been a dramatic improvement in the attitude of this parliament to the welfare of Canada's Indian population. This is keynoted by the basic gesture in a democracy of giving each Indian the vote. It is keynoted also by the stress on education that has been in evidence during the recent years, and keynoted by the policy of educational integration which is bringing together for the first time large segments of the Indian young people as they move into the classrooms of the public school system across the nation.

This program was implemented, I believe, in 1960. A reading of the latest report from the department of Indian affairs, I think it is found on page 16 of the report for 1962-63, reveals that up to 1962, 36 per cent of the Indian young people were accommodated in integrated schools across the land. I could talk about the rapid trend away from paternalism. This kind of administration of Indian affairs, which had removed responsibility from the reservation for so many years, has now been reversed. As a result of the elective system applied to band councils they are assuming more and more responsibility for the administration of their own internal problems. This of course will eventually lead to a situation where they have full responsibility as local municipal governments.
The education of the young people is not sufficient and education in integrated schools is not sufficient. It is dealing with the current situation, but there is a great backlog of young people who were educated under the old system. They were educated in residential schools, perhaps up to grade 7 or grade 8. Having learned the fundamentals of reading, writing and arithmetic, they returned to the reservation and their second state was worse than the first because they had become marginal people. They were not part of the main Canadian way of life, and they had received sufficient education to remove them from the way of life on a reservation. It became imperative, therefore, that they be included in the vocational training programs that were launched in 1960, particularly the educational upgrading program. It has been encouraging to note that in each of the classes, the vocational training classes and the educational upgrading classes that have been held in Canada over the past four years, there has been a good representation of our first Canadians.
I had the privilege of attending the first graduating class in my own city of Brandon last fall, when some 63 young people were graduated from the vocational training program launched in 1960, and amongst them were the children of residents of our Indian reservations. It is particularly interesting to note that before such students graduate they must have become successfully established in a useful occupation for a period of at least one year.
Then there is the question of adult education, and I took heart from the minister's recent announcement indicating a sum of money would be set aside to encourage community development programs on the reserva-

tions. This of course is a real fundamental attack on the problem of depressed social conditions. I hope this will mean the provision of community development officers on these reservations, and the provision of placement officers to act as counsellors in assisting these people to obtain gainful employment in the Canadian economy.
I also hope it will include the expansion of adult education programs. Very few reservations have organized adult education programs. Some excellent work is being conducted by voluntary groups, such as the friendship councils that have been referred to, which are developing rapidly in the major cities, but there should be something that would be tied into a formal educational program. I trust when the minister replies he will indicate that the progressive program launched by the former Conservative administration is being continued under the new administration.
It is interesting to note that there is a strong flavour in this of the kind of program undertaken by the department of northern affairs in recent years, dealing with Eskimo people. I am sure the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will agree with me on this point, that his department's program for Eskimos has included all these broad ramifications. I think it is not accidental that the same spirit is moving into the Indian affairs branch, because that branch has been successful in enticing from the department of northern affairs some of the key personnel who had been pioneering this program in the Canadian north.
I believe the time has come to make provision for school boards on reservations. It will be agreed that the system of giving more and more local responsibility to the band councils is proving highly successful, and now that they have grasped the nettle of local democracy for the first time the next step forward should be the provision of local school boards to handle the problems of schools which still remain on the reservations. This is one of the areas where I have had the greatest problems in the two reservations in my constituency, the Oak River and Oak Lake reservations. The Indians there would like to have some share in selecting their teachers. There is great mobility among the teaching profession on reservations, and they feel that they should have some say in the choice of teachers in order to get personnel more suitable for local prevailing conditions.

The time is not far removed when the remaining schools on the reservations will be staffed by Indian teachers. Now, with more and more young Indian people going into university and taking teacher training courses, this would be the ideal solution. Indian teachers would have a tremendous impact on the rising generation.
I could deal with many other subjects with respect to Indian affairs. I would like to reinforce the suggestion made by my colleague from Parry Sound-Muskoka, that it is high time we had a spokesman for the Indian population in the House of Commons. We have one in the upper house and I think all will concede that this has been a worthwhile development. I may also mention that the hon. members for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories have often suggested that there should be a spokesman for the Eskimo population in the house. This is something which is done in countries like New Zealand and Australia with reference to their aboriginal populations. Now that we are conscious of our obligations to these first Canadians, now that we have begun to move forward, this is a further step that would have a tremendous impact on their morale and on their gradual acceptance of full responsibility as citizens of Canada.
In summing up, in short discussions of this kind we always tend to generalize, and so I should like to underline a few points which we should recognize as pitfalls in the program presently being implemented. One of the great problems of the Indian reservations system is chronic poverty. People talk about the poverty of the underprivileged in the various countries around the world where refugee problems exist, but I do not think one could find conditions worse than those which exist in a good many of our own Indian reservations. Constituents of mine have become very exercised about this matter and have written asking what the government is doing about it. The only reply one can give to letters like that is to point out the government programs that do exist, and stress that if flesh and blood is to be put into these programs there must be initiative on the part of the local citizenry.
Carried.

I see my hon. friend from Lapointe is here this week and that he wants this particular matter to be carried. I have heard him wax long and eloquent on matters that are of particular interest to his own area. If he is going to be a first class Cana-

dian himself and think of the needs of Canada and Canadians generally, he would be well advised to give some attention to this extremely sensitive and difficult problem.
There is a problem of hard core poverty which should exercise the consciences of all of us. Unfortunately, this is a self-perpetuating problem. Where grinding poverty exists, it tends to become a way of life after two or three generations. The parents are poor, they are undereducated, they are underemployed, and they become dependant on public assistance. The same pattern will be followed by their children. They will be weakly motivated, they will drop out of school, they will be underemployed, and they in turn will be dependant on public assistance. The only way you can get at this rut is to approach it from several directions at once. Welfare workers now recognize the difficulty of the chronic problem family. You are not going to get at the problem by dealing in isolation with one smaller aspect; you must move in with all your welfare resources and tackle it right at the roots. Neither is education enough; it is not enough to say, "We have expanded educational facilities", just to salve our conscience. We in North America tend to believe that education will solve all problems, but education is only one tool. I am sure this is recognized by the government.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I think we have to recognize that wars are expensive, and the war on poverty is no exception. However, I think we will all agree that new interest and enthusiasm in tackling this problem is going to not only bring great immediate benefits to the people of Canada but will also be a rich investment for Canada's future. If we in this house forgot this business of harping so much on the rights of the founding races, on problems of racism in this country, and looked around and saw that we have a responsibility to Canadians whatever their ethnic or racial background, we would be making a large contribution to resolving the problems of these, our first Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take part in the debate; I just want to point out that it is excessively boring.
The chief whip of the Conservative party is going around with pills to keep the members of his party awake. I think that of all the evenings I have spent in the house, tonight is the worst, and I will ask the Conservative members to be kind enough to give us a chance to adopt the motion on interim supply, otherwise we will have to ask

the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) to take out of the interim supply we are dealing with tonight a portion of the federal grants to mental hospitals and to send the money to the Conservative caucus, because if they are listening to their own speeches tonight they will realize that they are erecting a monument to human stupidity.
This has been going on for five days. There are 265 members in the House of Commons. It seems to me that there are more important matters to discuss, namely the legislation to establish a department of agriculture for eastern Canada or of rural development, and several other bills. We would be ready to discuss those matters. But I keep hearing the same speakers repeating the same things. I feel the Conservatives should make an effort, if they are able, to pass interim supply, and then, if they so wish, sit all through summer -I am not against that-to do useful work. Let us give something to the country, but let us stop useless and fruitless discussions like those we have been hearing these last five or six days. It is a waste of time.
A moment ago, I was going over the measures still to be passed. There are many much more important than the ones under discussion at this time.
If the purpose of these discussions is to have us sit all summer, we are prepared to do just that, but let us discuss intelligently of matters which will benefit the country.
I think the Conservatives should be the first ones to allow us to do that.
The whip of that party gave me to understand earlier that there were still ten speakers on the roster. If they are going to be anything like the ones we have heard tonight I would ask him to spare us all that.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to stress the fact that standing order 5 provides that "every member is bound to attend the service of the house, unless leave of absence has been given him by the house." Now, I think the Liberals will agree with me that tonight's debate is one of the dullest we have had in a long time. Therefore, I would ask the house to give me leave of absence at least for the rest of the evening.
I have been here since eight o'clock. It has been an hour and a half-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that is an interesting interjection from hon. members opposite. I listened this evening to the hon.
[The Deputy Chairman.]

member for York-Scarborough first of all accuse people on this side of the house of prolonging debate-his precise words. Then he asked whether we knew he had spoken twice last Friday-which is quite true, but it was only to talk out, if I remember correctly, somebody else's bill. The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam, who today made the proposal to meet with the government side, called that intervention and that of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice Liberal hypocrisy at its best.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs made a contribution to the debate today. It is a peculiar thing, but in entering a debate like this, with the opposition endeavouring to do that which the government has not given it the opportunity to do, I am reminded of the actions of that minister when he sat on this side of the house. I am reminded of the great interest he, the great artist of doom and gloom, took in affairs of labour and employment. He produced his own bureau of statistics to prove that everything was bad and going down the drain, that everything was in tough shape. He also became a specialist in agriculture for southern Ontario. Now he seems to have forgotten all these things. Now that he thinks he is in a responsible position, everything is fine, and he is going to make it rough for us if we do not go along with him. That is the twist which events have taken today.
With other hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, I should like to compliment the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs in rising to answer questions regarding the contribution the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek made in regard to that department. I also noticed with interest that the parliamentary secretary said that it was his unpleasant duty to talk out the bill of the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.). If it was his duty, then he must have been instructed to do it. Therefore he did what he was supposed to do, against the interests of one of his own members. That is what we said at the time, in agreeing that the measure proposed by the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) was a very worthy one. I should like to repeat some of the words used that day in the debate on the hon. member's motion. He had this to say, as reported at page 4566 of Hansard:
Before entering the house today I was informed that the Canadian pension commission is being authorized to undertake the kind of survey to which I have just referred. I was of course pleased to hear this, since it was in order to encourage such a course that I placed my motion on the order

paper last February. However, I do not intend to ask that my motion be withdrawn. I feel that the two proposals-mine, and that of the veterans affairs committee-are complementary and I should like to feel that the members of this house through the committee on veterans affairs would have a hand in directing the course of the survey suggested.
We agreed at that time-and I think this was indicated today by the parliamentary secretary-that another course would have to be followed, had that measure been adopted. However, I do not think that is the case. At that time we had the same attitude that we have now, that the house should have been given the opportunity to be unanimous. As the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek said this evening, this is one of the best committees of the house as far as freedom from partisanship is concerned. Little partisanship if any is displayed in that committee. Therefore I feel that the minister and the government would have been wise to allow the entire house to give its approval not only to the suggestion concerning the pension commission but to the terms of the resolution as a whole, as proposed by the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.).
The reason I am entering the debate this evening is due to a press report which appeared at about the time of our discussion of that resolution. I regret now that I did not see fit to raise this as a question of privilege at the time so as to straighten matters out, but I did not believe it was that important. However, inasmuch as this opportunity now presents itself I wish to take advantage of it. A Canadian Press report quoted me as saying that special allowances should be paid to all former prisoners of war, not just to the Hong Kong veterans. That is not correct, Mr. Chairman, and that is not what I said. What I said was that I felt that equal treatment should be extended to prisoners, regardless of what theatre they served in. I said nothing about allowances. I did not want any selfish attitude to be projected in this respect.
However, at that time I did refer to several specific instances concerning comrades of mine who had passed away, and I alluded to the circumstances in most of these cases. I think that the members of the press gallery will be aware today that another colleague of mine passed away a few days ago under similar circumstances to those referred to in my speech, which is reported at page 4572 of Hansard for June 22. Mr. John Norman Harris was a writer of some note from the city of Toronto, and as I said was a comrade of mine in eastern Germany. Without any prior illinterim Supply
ness and under exactly the same set of circumstances to which I referred in that debate he just passed out of the picture when he was vacationing with his family in Vermont.
I wanted to take part in the debate this evening to correct the error which had been made in the report of the debate that day, and also to say that we are very pleased that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs has seen fit to be the first in the course of the last six days to rise to his feet and make some reply to our questions. I have just been informed that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has done the same. However, it is a peculiar thing that the parliamentary secretaries have to be carrying on this responsibility at this time, and it is regrettable that the ministers have not taken the responsibility for answering questions about the departments which have been discussed during the past week. I hope that in the time that is left there will be some greater measure of responsibility on the part of those ministers of the crown to examine the number of questions which have been put and that they will come forward with some of the answers. If they do not provide the opposition with the time to debate these matters they must realize that we must take this responsibility unto ourselves, because of the serious picture which we feel is presented to the Canadian scene.

Mr. Chairman, tonight I should like to commence discussing a new topic. The subject about which I wish to speak involves a question of government enterprise versus private enterprise and the extent to which this government believes it is the function of crown corporations to compete with private enterprise, the methods by which they may compete and the lengths to which they may go.
I am very happy tonight to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his seat because I know he has been very interested in this subject. I intend to refer specifically to the Northern Transportation Company as the crown corporation which provides the most striking example of the malaise I find in government circles today.
I should like to refer to this subject now, without deferring it for any length of time because of the indication of some urgency in an answer given to me by the minister several days ago, to the effect that the Northern Transportation Company has let tenders for the construction of a boat in Vancouver. This

Interim Supply
situation indicates to me that Northern Transportation Company intends to extend further its operation. I have reason to believe I will be able to show this committee that such further expansion of these operations can only be done at the expense of private enterprise. I have every reason to believe, and hope that I have the evidence to show the committee, that a private enterprise, Arctic Shipping Limited, will almost certainly be forced out of business by this continuing expansion. I think there is much evidence to show that pressure on the Yellowknife Transportation Company, the only other private shipper on the Mackenzie river, is going to increase in direct proportion to the expansion of Northern Transportation Company operations.
Mr. Chairman, I think every member of this committee with any regard for private enterprise should be interested in this subject. I realize I have referred to the tactics in respect of the Northern Transportation Company on grievance, and I am sure that members have noted the number of questions I have placed on the order paper in an attempt to obtain more and more information on this subject. I will indicate at this time that I have many more questions now on the order paper in the hope that the answers will provide evidence enabling every member to understand fully the situation as it exists today.
Never before in this chamber have I had the opportunity of referring to this subject in chronological order. I think members will be interested in the position of the government in respect of crown corporations as it relates to the intention enunciated in this chamber at the time the corporations were established. I am sure that a consideration of the growth and purpose of these corporations together with a consideration of the type of operations they are carrying out, their extent of growth and changing conditions, will enable members to appreciate that the original purposes have been served in many instances.
We are faced with a situation in which there has been the creation of a giant which has accumulated so much equipment it must compete more and more strongly with private enterprise to put that equipment into useful operation. In other words by degrees and stages, and by various means, the government has slipped into the habit of allowing crown corporations to expand further and further in competition wtih private enterprise.

Some of the things we must consider are: What was the original policy? How far have these corporations grown? How far have we departed from the original policy? What is the change in the concept of the functions of some of these companies? What is the policy of these corporations as enunciated by the companies and government? What is the extent of resources behind crown corporations? How much can these corporations accumulate? How much of the taxpayers' dollar can be stated to be legitimate capital of the corporation, which the corporation can plan to use? Is there any limit in this regard? What tactics can management of crown corporations use in competition with private enterprise? What should be done with crown corporations set up for one purpose, when that purpose is found to be no longer necessary? When do we stop empire building in the civil service? What is the method of hiring as compared to private enterprise? In this connection what steps have been taken to implement the recommendations contained in the report by a parliamentary committee which spent a whole session studying this situation?
At the commencement of my remarks I should like to state that I realize the continued growth in activity of Northern Transportation Company has taken place during the last several years. The previous government did at least refer part of this problem to a special committee on research. I will also show that the situation involving the L.S.M. Sally being brought into Canada did not come to the attention of the government until just about the time of the change of government, and this government did exactly what the previous government did. The previous government did not pass an order in council allowing that ship in, when it should not have been allowed in through normal channels. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce was approached he also refrained from taking the necessary steps to have the order in council issued as requested by Northern Transportation Company.
Part of the difficulty which exists today, as it existed when the Conservatives were in power, resulted from the gradual expansion in the activities of crown corporations. I am sure the accumulation of equipment was carried out for legitimate purposes. This equipment was acquired to carry out jobs which the corporations were instructed to undertake and the growth took place stage by stage. The gradual encroachment in the field of private enterprise was accidental rather than planned, and took place by degrees rather than as a

result of a sudden change in government policy. I do not think anyone in government two years ago would have been prepared to enunciate government policy in this regard. As a result of answers I have obtained from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to which I will refer later, and as a result of physical statistics that have been supplied in relation to the changing situation in the north, I do not think the present minister can clearly enunciate policy in relation to the activities of this company.
When crown corporations were first established by Mr. C. D. Howe in 1946 the concept was that they should carry out essential government services not being provided by private enterprise. Private enterprise either did not exist, or did not or could not undertake a task in the realm of public interest which the government felt necessary, as the result of which the government found it necessary to provide these essential services. In 1946 during a debate in respect of crown corporations Mr. Howe had the following to say as reported at page 2176 of Hansard for that year:
-it has never created a company that is in competition with private business in any way, shape or manner. If private business was able to carry out the war objective, private business was given that opportunity. The government has created crown companies only to undertake work that private industry was not willing to undertake.
Mr. Howe then went on to say:
I know of no government company that has ever been in direct competition with private industry; and certainly those that will be continuing companies cannot possibly be considered to be in competition with private industry.
I think that quotation makes my initial point very clear. I am sure that the Liberal party regards itself as a free enterprise party, as does the Conservative party. I know the Creditistes and the Social Credit party make much of this point, and I am sure the members of the New Democratic party are interested in this subject, perhaps not because they are against direct competition as such, but because of a desire to make sure that government enterprises are run efficiently and fairly, and compete on a basis under which competition is honest and fair without the use of undue influence by crown corporations as a result of the positions they occupy.
When 1 have referred to this matter previously in the house I have not bothered to make the statement that my argument is not based on a lack of efficiency on the part of the personnel of Northern Transportation Company compared with Yellowknife Transportation Company. Both companies have a very 20220-401

good reputation in the north for service and the individuals employed by them are efficient and hard working. Certainly if the people in any crown corporation did not work hard and efficiently in carrying out their duties to make their company the best they could, they would be doing less than what they are required to do.
I have no quarrel with that aspect. My quarrel and my argument concern government policy. They concern the top public servants who run the company and advise the government on policy and the top civil servants who advise the minister on policy. It is the change from the policy as indicated by C. D. Howe to the present policy, which is not so much enunciated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as indicated by the activities of the company, that I should like to emphasize tonight.
It might be a good starting point to refer to the matter of policy as enunciated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when I have queried him about it in the house. On the 4th of October, 1963, I put a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on policy. It is to be found on page 3208 of Hansard for that year and the last part of the question reads as follows:
Does the government intend to permit Northern Transportation Company to extend its operations in the north in direct competition with private enterprise?
The minister replied as follows:
This is a question of which I would require some notice. As the hon. gentleman knows, there have been discussions between the Northern Transportation Company and some of the other carriers. We have had this matter under consideration for some time, and I think it would be in the interests of all concerned if I had a little time to prepare an answer which would be as clear and satisfactory as possible.
I then asked the following clarifying question:
Is it true the minister is being advised on this question by a committee composed of his deputy and the president of Northern Transportation Company, although the question being considered is the competition between Northern Transportation Company and private enterprise in the north?
This was the answer:
I can assure the hon. gentleman that I am receiving advice from many quarters, including those he has mentioned.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I question the source of his advice. I cannot see how the minister can feel that any advice he would get from the people in charge of Northern Transportation Company or the president of Eldorado Mining and Refining in response to the complaints that I and many others have

brought to his attention could be anything other than that this situation is healthy for the company and that this is the proper method of proceeding. I might say that in a minute I am going to refer to the further answer given by the minister, but the question of policy, whether further expansion in competition is going to be allowed, has not been clearly enunciated yet.
Some time ago some assurance was given by the minister to the president of Arctic Shipping and the president of Yellowknife Transportation when Northern Transportation took over the Hudson's Bay Company boat, the Banksland. At one time the Hudson's Bay Company turned over to Northern Transportation Company its facilities on the Mackenzie river, and then a year or two ago sold the Banksland to Northern Transportation Company. Up to this point there had been no operation in the Arctic as such by Northern Transportation Company, other than the operation which that company had carried on in connection with supplying the D.E.W. line.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce gave the assurance to Arctic Shipping and to Yellowknife Transportation Company that this did not mean the expansion of the services provided by Northern Transportation in the Arctic and that all they were doing was to take over the business that had been done by the Hudson's Bay Company. This is the first point where I think the minister must have been misled, or else the company did gradually expand after he had given that answer.
Up to that point there had been no bulk oil shipments handled in the Arctic by either the Hudson's Bay Company or Northern Transportation Company. But not only did Northern Transportation Company take over the Banksland; they started hauling barges behind it, a type of service never before provided. They started to go into areas where the Hudson's Bay Company had never gone. In other words, the minister had received assurances from these people that this did not in fact constitute an expansion of the service when in fact it did; and I am sure the reason he answered as he did was that he did not know about this business of shipping in the Arctic.
I can recall the fuss that was raised when, after Yellowknife Transportation Company had made their plans to carry certain shipments of oil and it was so far advanced in the season it was too late for them to re-

arrange things, that company was summarily dismissed because another department had already issued orders that the Hudson's Bay Company would carry this oil. Of course, the policy in the Arctic had always been that the transportation of oil would be given to Yellowknife or Arctic Shipping or Hudson's Bay and that Hudson's Bay Company was entitled to half the business. As it turned out, however, Hudson's Bay Company never had the equipment or never really used it and in fact Arctic Shipping had always done the work.
What happened when Northern Transportation took over? They said it was always intended that Hudson's Bay Company would get half of the business so they were not expanding. Certainly this is a specious argument in view of the fact that Arctic Shipping had been struggling to provide a service in the Arctic and had become accustomed to carrying this business, because it found too late in the season for it to do anything about it that the situation had changed. In the first year their anticipated income was knocked down by $30,000. I do not think this is a minor thing because Arctic Shipping cannot stand that type of competition. It cannot stand losing that amount of business.
I believe most members feel that the government should encourage private enterprise to open up the north and that it is necessary for this purpose that private companies remain strong and healthy. The deliberate expansion of the facilities of Northern Transportation at the expense of a small company is simply going to cripple that small company and this matter must be looked at most seriously by the government.
I hope I do not do the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources an injustice when I now state what I believe he has stated to be the policy of the government with regard to helping open up the north. I know he is very sincere in his interest in that area and I certainly am convinced from what he has said that he is much in favour of private enterprise. His view seems to be that the role of the government is to provide those services which private enterprise cannot or will not provide, that where it is advantageous and will help to open up the north if the government moves in the government should do so. I think he would probably go further and say the government should not be too slow in moving in there.
But I have never heard him make any statement of policy that is in line with what is actually happening in the Arctic today.

I refer again to C. D. Howe's statement of policy under which it was laid down that crown corporations after they are established are not intended to be in competition with private enterprise. In other words, even on the view of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources with regard to the role of government enterprise in the north, they are only intended to fill that gap that private enterprise cannot or will not fill, or to enter into the picture if private enterprise is slow moving. Certainly, nothing less than this is going to be of assistance. Nothing has been said by the minister of northern affairs, and I will give him time to correct me right now. I want to be fair, and I am glad that he is in his seat tonight.
I should like to refer now to some of the other problems we have in connection with these companies. As I said, I think the reason we now have the problems we have today, where competition is so fierce that one private shipper is going to be frozen out of the Arctic, is directly due to the growth and expansion of this company. The purpose for which this growth was allowed was not to permit the company to be in competition with private enterprise. To begin with, Northern Transportation is a subsidiary of Eldorado Mining. It was required to look after the mine and provide the hauling available in the north. There was just not sufficient private enterprise available to make sure the government's mining program could be carried out. Eldorado was charged with the duty of providing tugs and barges so that this function could be carried out. I have no quarrel with that; it was necessary.
There was another instance of growth in connection with the D.E.W. line supplies. Northern Transportation Company was made the official agent of government to make sure that there would be sufficient transportation available for the building of the D.E.W. line stations. I may say that when Northern Transportation was so. appointed, its duty was to act as the voice of the private carriers as well as the government. It was really supposed to survey the transportation facilities then available, to co-ordinate those private facilities and to plan such other facilities as it felt were necessary in order that there might be sufficient service to carry out this work.
When we are considering the growth of these companies, I think it is well to remind ourselves that Northern Transportation-here is where the empire building came in- ignored the private facilities then available 20220-401J

in Canada. At that time Yellowknife Transportation Company, which since the depression had been struggling to provide a service in the north, had a tug or two and several barges surplus to business on hand. The company could not get enough business to keep them busy. It would have been of considerable assistance had Northern Transportation Company, by reason of being the agent of the government, made use of this equipment and given private enterprise a chance to share in the growth of the transportation business that was going to result from the defence construction. This company was completely ignored and all that business was handled by Northern Transportation Company. The other companies could struggle as much as they wanted.
I cannot imagine any other sphere of activity in Canada, whether it be aircraft production or the production of any other supplies for the armed services where, if a certain crown agency had a duty to survey the material available and to act as spokesman for those engaged in the industry supplying that material, the crown agency would be allowed to ignore private Canadian enterprise and set up its own company to handle this business. This is the equivalent of what has happened in this case. Then, you would have the equivalent of the crown organization ending up with a huge fleet and edging over to compete for the private business in the north in competition with private enterprise.
Certainly, I believe this might be the appropriate time to comment on the method by which businesses can grow and expand. Every company, especially those we like to think form the backbone of this country, is set up by men of daring, vision and imagination who are willing to get in there and slug. They generally have to build out of profits. Certainly, if such a company is going to meet competition from a competitor who has unlimited capital resources, then they are in trouble. This is now the situation on Mackenzie river and in the Arctic. We have a crown corporation with millions of dollars worth of equipment and with all the resources of the government behind it competing on the Mackenzie river with Yellowknife Transportation, which is struggling to build itself up.
Yellowknife Transportation is now a respectably sized company but it still has to have due regard for the amount of capital required when it is going to plan its facilities. To illustrate this fact, I think we only have to repeat the story of the L.S.M. Sally.
I brought this question up on a grievance

period, but perhaps in view of what I have said the story may make a little more sense to hon. members now. The L.S.M. Sally was a government surplus war ship purchased by Northern Transportation Company and brought into Vancouver. Since it is quite old it was unable to pass the maritime regulations which prohibit a boat more than five years old being brought into the area for use. They could not get a licence. Yellowknife Transportation tried to do the same thing three years before. Yellowknife thought they could use this boat to advantage, and since it was old they believed the amount of capital required could be financed. The company believed it may be the best way of providing equipment to take care of expansion. When Yellowknife tried this three years before and found they could not do it, they had to make alternative plans. They built additional tugs and barges to take care of the business for which they could have used the L.S.M.
Now, Northern Transportation meets the same situation. They cannot use the Sally. What does the minister's latest communication tell me they are going to do? They have tenders out to build a new boat. They first tried to accomplish their purpose the sneaky way, I submit, by trying to get an order in council passed so they would be above the ordinary law to which Yellowknife Transportation was subject. Failing that, they have allowed this ship to stay in Vancouver harbour for a year and a half. The company now has tenders out for a new hull. They will take the insides out of the Sally and put them in the new hull, thereby getting the same type of ship without the expense of building it all from scratch.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that only a government agency could afford this sort of thing. Northern Transportation Company has, of this date, 97 barges licensed to cover the Athabasca and Mackenzie sectors. I am not sure how many tugs they have. I do know, according to figures supplied in an answer given me by the minister, that only 89 of these barges were used last year. One or two were leased out to Yellowknife Transportation. What is more, an examination of the figures relating to the total tons hauled by the two companies shows that Yellowknife Transportation company hauled a greater tonnage with only half the barges. This is the situation we are facing today. I say again every member in this house, including the minister, will want to look at the situation closely. What private enterprise company can afford to do business this way? Having invested in

more barges than were needed, Northern Transportation is going ahead to make a further investment in this type of ship.
I would like to refer now to the minister's subsequent statement on policy that he gave to the house on October 9. It is fairly long but I want to read it all because I think it is only proper in the context of this speech that his statement be complete. Then I shall refer to it bit by bit later. It appears at page 3369 of Hansard for October 9, 1963, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go contrary to your advice with regard to the answer to this question-
I had a little trouble with the Speaker in getting him to recognize the question as urgent, which explains the minister's opening remarks.
-but I do owe an answer to the hon. member which I think I perhaps should make now.
